Reference-based sensitivity analysis for bounded longitudinal outcomes

Abstract

Reference-based sensitivity analysis is widely used to assess departures from the assumption that data are missing at random in longitudinal randomized trials, but existing methods are typically formulated for approximately Gaussian continuous outcomes and do not directly accommodate bounded outcomes, particularly when exact lower or upper bounds may occur with appreciable probability. We propose a Bayesian reference-based sensitivity analysis framework for bounded longitudinal outcomes, based on a thresholded latent Gaussian working model. Interior observations are mapped one-to-one to the latent scale, whereas boundary observations correspond to latent values below or above prespecified thresholds, yielding a distribution on the observed scale with a continuous interior density and positive mass at the bounds. Reference-based rules are imposed on the latent scale, and posterior predictive imputation proceeds on that scale before mapping back to the original outcome scale. Simulations assessed model calibration, recovery of complete data contrasts, and population treatment effect inference after imputation. For the proposed model, population treatment effect inference showed small bias when the analysis rule matched the truth rule after the trigger, but conservative Rubin intervals, particularly under jump to reference. The method is illustrated using the BtheB study, a longitudinal trial with a bounded depression outcome and incomplete follow-up.

Keywords: reference-based sensitivity analysis; bounded longitudinal outcomes; controlled multiple imputation; missing data; latent Gaussian model

1 Introduction

Missing data arising after treatment discontinuation, dropout, or other deviations after randomization remain a central challenge in the analysis of longitudinal randomized trials. Sensitivity analyses assess how conclusions depend on assumptions about unobserved outcomes that cannot be verified from the observed data alone (ICH,, 2020; EMA,, 2010). Reference-based multiple imputation (RBMI) constructs distributions for missing outcomes in the active arm using information from a reference arm, usually the control group (Carpenter et al.,, 2013; Cro et al.,, 2020). Under conventional Gaussian formulations, jump to reference (J2R) specifies a marginal mean trajectory that follows the active arm before a specified trigger and the reference arm afterward, with imputation then conditional on the available outcome history. Copy reference (CR) instead uses the reference arm conditional distribution given the available outcome history. Weighted rules interpolate between the conditional means under missing at random (MAR) and J2R. These approaches provide structured alternatives to MAR whose suitability depends on the clinical setting and the treatment effect of interest.

Most reference-based methods have been developed for continuous longitudinal outcomes under Gaussian or multivariate normal working models, closely related to mixed models or analyses of repeated measures under MAR (Mallinckrodt et al.,, 2003; Mallinckrodt et al.,, 2008; Carpenter et al.,, 2013; Cro et al.,, 2020). This framework is familiar and convenient, but it is less satisfactory when the outcome is known to lie within a fixed support. Many trial endpoints are bounded, including symptom scores, questionnaire totals, proportions, and related indices. In such settings, direct Gaussian imputation can generate values outside the allowable range, motivating transformations, models that respect the bounds, or adjustments to the imputed values (Geraci and McLain,, 2018; Rodwell et al.,, 2014).

Several model classes have been proposed for bounded outcomes, including latent variable and coarsening models for bounded scores (Lesaffre et al.,, 2007; Molas and Lesaffre,, 2008; Xu et al.,, 2014), beta regression models with random effects or mixtures (Verkuilen and Smithson,, 2012), and models that place explicit mass at one or both bounds through inflated beta or related augmented beta rectangular constructions (Ospina and Ferrari,, 2010; Wang and Luo,, 2016; Wang and Luo,, 2017). These approaches are useful for modeling bounded responses, but they were not developed with the simple conditional multivariate normal imputation formulas used in conventional reference-based sensitivity analysis in mind. At the same time, recent work has started to extend reference-based sensitivity analysis beyond the standard Gaussian setting for continuous outcomes, for example, to right-censored time-to-event outcomes and longitudinal binary outcomes (Atkinson et al.,, 2021; Lu,, 2020; Cro et al.,, 2025). To our knowledge, however, no existing reference-based framework combines a continuous interior distribution and explicit mass at the bounds for bounded longitudinal outcomes with Gaussian completion (imputation) on the latent scale.

In this paper, we extend reference-based sensitivity analysis to bounded longitudinal outcomes by using a thresholded latent Gaussian working model. Interior observations are mapped one-to-one to a latent Gaussian scale, whereas observations at the lower and upper bounds correspond to latent values below or above prespecified thresholds. This induces a distribution on the observed scale with a continuous interior density and positive mass at the bounds. The reference-based rules are imposed on the latent scale, where the familiar Gaussian completion formulas remain available. Missing outcomes are completed by posterior predictive sampling on the latent scale and then mapped back to the observed scale, so completed values automatically respect the support and can equal the bounds exactly.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the motivating BtheB example. Section 3 introduces the observed data structure and support specification. Section 4 develops the thresholded latent Gaussian framework and the reference-based completion rules. Section 5 presents the simulation studies. Section 6 presents the application to the BtheB data, and Section 7 concludes.

2 Motivating data example

We illustrate the proposed framework using the BtheB data, available in the HSAUR2 package and originating from a randomized primary care trial comparing the computerized cognitive behavioral therapy program Beating the Blues (BtheB) with treatment as usual (TAU) (Proudfoot et al.,, 2003; Hothorn and Everitt,, 2025). The Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) was measured at baseline and at 2, 3, 5, and 8 months post-baseline. In the methodological development below, the longitudinal outcome vector comprises the four post-baseline measurements, indexed by t=1,…,4t=1,\dots,4 for the 2-, 3-, 5-, and 8-month visits. The BDI-II is a bounded integer score taking values from 00 to 6363.

The publicly available HSAUR2 dataset contains 100 subjects, of whom 48 were assigned to TAU and 52 to BtheB. For the present application, we excluded 3 TAU subjects with no post-baseline BDI-II measurements, leaving 97 subjects for analysis, with 45 in TAU and 52 in BtheB. Over follow-up, the observed mean profiles suggest improvement in both groups, with a more pronounced decline in the BtheB arm; see Web Figure 1 in Web Appendix A of the Supporting Information. This same pattern is visible in Figure 1, where the BtheB arm shows a progressively greater concentration of lower scores during follow-up. The original trial used a frequentist linear mixed model under MAR, with covariate adjustment and random intercepts and slopes for each subject (Proudfoot et al.,, 2003). The estimated BtheB versus TAU difference, assumed common across visits after treatment, was −5.21-5.21 BDI-II points (95% CI: −8.60-8.60 to −1.82-1.82). No formal intercurrent event strategy was specified. Our analysis illustrates missing data sensitivity using the publicly available dataset rather than reproducing the original analysis.

Two features of these data motivate the proposed methodology. First, the outcome is bounded, and the lower bound is reached in practice. Exact zero values occur with appreciable frequency and become more prominent later in follow-up; see Web Figure 2. Second, longitudinal follow-up is incomplete in the retained analysis set. Missingness is negligible at baseline and increases substantially over the post-baseline visits in both arms, approaching half by 8 months; see Figure 2. Subject trajectories likewise show incomplete follow-up for many subjects before the final visit; see Web Figure 3.

Taken together, the BtheB data illustrate the central practical problem addressed in this paper: standard Gaussian longitudinal models do not naturally accommodate bounded outcomes together with appreciable probability at the boundary and incomplete follow-up.

3 Observed data structure and support specification

Consider a longitudinal randomized trial with subjects indexed by i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n and scheduled post-baseline visits indexed by t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T. Let Yi​tY_{it} denote the outcome of interest for subject ii at visit tt, and let Ai∈{0,1}A_{i}\in\left\{0,1\right\} denote randomized treatment assignment, where Ai=1A_{i}=1 indicates the active arm and Ai=0A_{i}=0 the reference arm. Let Xi​tX_{it} denote the covariate vector entering the longitudinal mean model, which may include baseline outcome, visit indicators, interactions between baseline outcome and visit, stratification factors, and other prognostic variables. Write XiX_{i} for the collection of covariates for subject ii across all visits. Define the observation indicator

Ri​t={1,if ​Yi​t​ is observed,0,if ​Yi​t​ is missing.R_{it}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }Y_{it}\text{ is observed},\\ 0,&\text{if }Y_{it}\text{ is missing}.\end{cases} (2)

For subject ii, let LiL_{i} and UiU_{i} denote known finite bounds with Li<UiL_{i}<U_{i}, such that Li≤Yi​t≤UiL_{i}\leq Y_{it}\leq U_{i} for t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T. Although many applications share common bounds across subjects, we allow limits that vary across subjects to ensure generality.

For each subject, define the observed lower bound, interior, upper bound, and missing visit sets by

ℒi={t∈{1,…,T}:Ri​t=1,Yi​t=Li},\mathcal{L}_{i}=\left\{t\in\left\{1,\dots,T\right\}:R_{it}=1,Y_{it}=L_{i}\right\}, (3)
ℐi={t∈{1,…,T}:Ri​t=1,Li<Yi​t<Ui},\mathcal{I}_{i}=\left\{t\in\left\{1,\dots,T\right\}:R_{it}=1,L_{i}<Y_{it}<U_{i}\right\}, (4)
𝒰i={t∈{1,…,T}:Ri​t=1,Yi​t=Ui},\mathcal{U}_{i}=\left\{t\in\left\{1,\dots,T\right\}:R_{it}=1,Y_{it}=U_{i}\right\}, (5)

and

ℳi={t∈{1,…,T}:Ri​t=0}.\mathcal{M}_{i}=\left\{t\in\left\{1,\dots,T\right\}:R_{it}=0\right\}. (6)

The full observed visit index set is therefore 𝒪i=ℒi∪ℐi∪𝒰i\mathcal{O}_{i}=\mathcal{L}_{i}\cup\mathcal{I}_{i}\cup\mathcal{U}_{i}.

Let τi∈{1,…,T+1}\tau_{i}\in\left\{1,\dots,T+1\right\} denote the first visit from which the sensitivity assumption applies for subject ii, with τi=T+1\tau_{i}=T+1 if no such visit occurs. We restrict the reference-based formulation to a final missing tail: when τi≤T\tau_{i}\leq T, all outcomes from visit τi\tau_{i} onward are missing. An intercurrent event may define the trigger when all outcomes from the first affected visit onward are missing; otherwise, the trigger may be defined from the observed follow-up pattern as the visit immediately after the last observed outcome. Intermittent missing outcomes before the trigger are permitted. We then define the sets of missing visits before the trigger and from the trigger onward by

ℳipre=ℳi∩{1,…,τi−1},\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}=\mathcal{M}_{i}\cap\left\{1,\dots,\tau_{i}-1\right\}, (7)

and

ℳipost=ℳi∩{τi,…,T}.\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}=\mathcal{M}_{i}\cap\left\{\tau_{i},\dots,T\right\}. (8)

Here, ℳipre\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}} is empty when τi=1\tau_{i}=1, and ℳipost\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}} is empty when τi=T+1\tau_{i}=T+1.

The reference-based sensitivity assumptions introduced below apply only to the predictive distribution of missing values in the active arm from the trigger onward.

In the BtheB application considered below, intercurrent events are not recorded for individual subjects, so τi\tau_{i} is defined from the observed follow-up pattern rather than from an observed intercurrent event.

4 Methodology

We propose a reference-based sensitivity analysis framework for bounded longitudinal outcomes with possible exact boundary values. The key device is a thresholded latent Gaussian construction that combines a continuous interior distribution with positive mass at the bounds. We first introduce the representation on the observed scale and the model on the latent working scale, and then show how familiar reference-based assumptions can be imposed within that framework.

4.1 Thresholded Gaussian representation on the latent working scale

Motivated by latent variable threshold formulations for non-Gaussian longitudinal outcomes and related work on bounded outcomes, we introduce the following thresholded latent Gaussian representation (Lu,, 2020; Geraci and McLain,, 2018; Aguirre-Larracoechea and Borges,, 2021).

Let Hi​t∈ℝH_{it}\in\mathbb{R} denote a variable on the latent working scale and let ai<bia_{i}<b_{i} denote fixed lower and upper thresholds. It is convenient to define these through two prespecified constants pLip_{L_{i}} and pUip_{U_{i}} satisfying 0<pLi<pUi<10<p_{L_{i}}<p_{U_{i}}<1, with

ai=Φ−1​(pLi)andbi=Φ−1​(pUi),a_{i}=\Phi^{-1}\left(p_{L_{i}}\right)\qquad\text{and}\qquad b_{i}=\Phi^{-1}\left(p_{U_{i}}\right), (9)

where Φ\Phi denotes the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF).

The observed outcome is linked to the latent scale through

Yi​t={Li,if ​Hi​t≤ai,Li+(Ui−Li)​Φ⁡(Hi​t)−pLipUi−pLi,if ​ai<Hi​t<bi,Ui,if ​Hi​t≥bi.Y_{it}=\begin{cases}L_{i},&\text{if }H_{it}\leq a_{i},\\ L_{i}+\left(U_{i}-L_{i}\right)\dfrac{\Phi\left(H_{it}\right)-p_{L_{i}}}{p_{U_{i}}-p_{L_{i}}},&\text{if }a_{i}<H_{it}<b_{i},\\ U_{i},&\text{if }H_{it}\geq b_{i}.\end{cases} (10)

This induces positive mass at the lower bound LiL_{i} and the upper bound UiU_{i}, together with a continuous density on the interior (Li,Ui)\left(L_{i},U_{i}\right). The constants pLip_{L_{i}} and pUip_{U_{i}} specify fixed latent thresholds using the standard normal CDF; this does not require the latent outcome itself to have a standard normal distribution. If Hi​tH_{it} were standard normal, the probabilities of the lower and upper bounds would be pLip_{L_{i}} and 1−pUi1-p_{U_{i}}, respectively. More generally, under the Gaussian working model below, the boundary probabilities depend on the latent mean and standard deviation (SD) and can therefore vary even when the thresholds remain fixed.

For interior observations Yi​t∈(Li,Ui)Y_{it}\in\left(L_{i},U_{i}\right), the inverse map to the latent scale is

Hi​t=gi​(Yi​t)=Φ−1​(pLi+(pUi−pLi)​Yi​t−LiUi−Li).H_{it}=g_{i}\left(Y_{it}\right)=\Phi^{-1}\left(p_{L_{i}}+\left(p_{U_{i}}-p_{L_{i}}\right)\frac{Y_{it}-L_{i}}{U_{i}-L_{i}}\right). (11)

The corresponding Jacobian factor for a single interior observation is

|∂Hi​t∂Yi​t|=pUi−pLiUi−Li​1ϕ⁡(Hi​t),\left|\frac{\partial H_{it}}{\partial Y_{it}}\right|=\frac{p_{U_{i}}-p_{L_{i}}}{U_{i}-L_{i}}\frac{1}{\phi\left(H_{it}\right)}, (12)

where ϕ\phi denotes the standard normal density.

The thresholds aia_{i} and bib_{i} may be chosen to suit the application. For outcomes recorded on a discrete score grid with step size sis_{i}, a natural choice is

pLi=si/2Ui−Li+siandpUi=1−si/2Ui−Li+si.p_{L_{i}}=\frac{s_{i}/2}{U_{i}-L_{i}+s_{i}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad p_{U_{i}}=1-\frac{s_{i}/2}{U_{i}-L_{i}+s_{i}}. (13)

This choice corresponds to extending the score range by half a step at each end when defining the probit rescaling. For integer scores with si=1s_{i}=1, the interior transformation becomes

gi​(y)=Φ−1​(y−Li+0.5Ui−Li+1),Li<y<Ui.g_{i}\left(y\right)=\Phi^{-1}\left(\frac{y-L_{i}+0.5}{U_{i}-L_{i}+1}\right),\qquad L_{i}<y<U_{i}. (14)

Thus, interior observations use the familiar midpoint correction, while exact boundary observations are represented by latent tail events. As pLip_{L_{i}} approaches 00 and pUip_{U_{i}} approaches 11, the thresholded observation rule reduces in the limit to a purely continuous probit transformation, with no probability mass at either bound.

Let Hi=(Hi​1,…,Hi​T)⊤H_{i}=\left(H_{i1},\dots,H_{iT}\right)^{\top} denote the vector on the latent working scale for subject ii. Under the primary analysis model, we assume

Hi|Ai=a,Xi,θ∼𝒩(μi​a,Σa),a∈{0,1},H_{i}\left|A_{i}=a,X_{i},\theta\right.\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\mu_{ia},\Sigma_{a}\right),\qquad a\in\left\{0,1\right\}, (15)

where μi​a\mu_{ia} is the mean vector for arm aa, Σa\Sigma_{a} is the covariance matrix for repeated outcomes within a subject in that arm, and θ\theta denotes the full collection of model parameters. Although this notation allows covariance matrices to differ between arms, the reference-based rules, theoretical results, and numerical analyses presented here use a common latent covariance matrix, Σ0=Σ1=Σ\Sigma_{0}=\Sigma_{1}=\Sigma.

For any visit index set 𝒥⊆{1,…,T}\mathcal{J}\subseteq\left\{1,\dots,T\right\}, let Hi,𝒥H_{i,\mathcal{J}} denote the subvector of HiH_{i} containing the components indexed by 𝒥\mathcal{J}, arranged in increasing visit order. Likewise, μi​a,𝒥\mu_{ia,\mathcal{J}} denotes the corresponding subvector of μi​a\mu_{ia}. For visit index sets 𝒥,𝒦⊆{1,…,T}\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}\subseteq\left\{1,\dots,T\right\}, let Σa,𝒥​𝒦\Sigma_{a,\mathcal{J}\mathcal{K}} denote the submatrix of Σa\Sigma_{a} formed by the rows indexed by 𝒥\mathcal{J} and the columns indexed by 𝒦\mathcal{K}.

A flexible visit-specific mean specification is

μi​a=(μi​a​1,…,μi​a​T)⊤,μi​a​t=Xi​t⊤βt+aWi​t⊤δt,t=1,…,T,\mu_{ia}=\left(\mu_{ia1},\dots,\mu_{iaT}\right)^{\top},\qquad\mu_{iat}=X_{it}^{\top}\beta_{t}+aW_{it}^{\top}\delta_{t},\qquad t=1,\dots,T, (16)

where βt\beta_{t} contains visit-specific prognostic effects and δt\delta_{t} contains visit-specific treatment effects. In many applications, Wi​tW_{it} may simply be a subset of Xi​tX_{it} corresponding to interactions between treatment and visit.

To illustrate the thresholded construction, consider the special case with common support, Li=0L_{i}=0, Ui=63U_{i}=63, and si=1s_{i}=1 for all subjects, so that the thresholds are also common across subjects. For a single visit, suppose Hi​t∼𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)H_{it}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\mu,\sigma^{2}\right) with the representative setting (μ,σ)=(−1.1,1.0)\left(\mu,\sigma\right)=\left(-1.1,1.0\right). Under the thresholded model, this induces approximately Pr⁡(Yi​t=Li)=0.09\Pr\left(Y_{it}=L_{i}\right)=0.09 and Pr⁡(Yi​t=Ui)=0.00\Pr\left(Y_{it}=U_{i}\right)=0.00. Figure 3 displays the corresponding Gaussian density on the latent scale, the threshold locations, and the induced distribution on the observed scale.

4.2 Primary posterior under missing at random

Under the baseline MAR imputation model, outcome missingness is assumed to depend only on observed outcomes, treatment assignment, and observed covariates. The parameters governing missingness are assumed to be distinct from, and a priori independent of, θ\theta, so the missingness mechanism can be ignored in posterior inference. Boundary observations are handled through latent augmentation. Interior observations determine latent values exactly through the inverse map gi​(⋅)g_{i}\left(\cdot\right), whereas observations at the lower and upper bounds imply only that the corresponding latent variables satisfy Hi​t≤aiH_{it}\leq a_{i} and Hi​t≥biH_{it}\geq b_{i}. We therefore adopt a latent data augmentation strategy in Stan (Carpenter et al.,, 2017).

For subject ii, define the augmented observed latent vector H~i,𝒪i=(H~i​t:t∈𝒪i)⊤\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}}=\left(\widetilde{H}_{it}:t\in\mathcal{O}_{i}\right)^{\top}, where

H~i​t={Hi​t,if ​t∈ℐi,Hi​tL,if ​t∈ℒi,Hi​tU,if ​t∈𝒰i,\widetilde{H}_{it}=\begin{cases}H_{it},&\text{if }t\in\mathcal{I}_{i},\\ H_{it}^{L},&\text{if }t\in\mathcal{L}_{i},\\ H_{it}^{U},&\text{if }t\in\mathcal{U}_{i},\end{cases} (17)

with constraints Hi​tL≤aiH_{it}^{L}\leq a_{i} for t∈ℒit\in\mathcal{L}_{i} and Hi​tU≥biH_{it}^{U}\geq b_{i} for t∈𝒰it\in\mathcal{U}_{i}. Thus, interior components are known exactly from the observed data, whereas boundary components are latent and sampled jointly with the model parameters.

Up to multiplicative terms that are constant with respect to θ\theta and the boundary latent variables, the augmented posterior under MAR is

p(θ,{Hi​tL:t∈ℒi,i=1,…,n},{Hi​tU:t∈𝒰i,i=1,…,n}|𝒟obs)\displaystyle p\left(\theta,\left\{H_{it}^{L}:t\in\mathcal{L}_{i},\;i=1,\dots,n\right\},\left\{H_{it}^{U}:t\in\mathcal{U}_{i},\;i=1,\dots,n\right\}\middle|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right) (18)
∝p(θ)∏i=1n[p(H~i,𝒪i|Ai,Xi,θ)𝟙(Hi,ℒiL≤ai𝟏)𝟙(Hi,𝒰iU≥bi𝟏)].\displaystyle\propto p\left(\theta\right)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left[p\left(\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}}\middle|A_{i},X_{i},\theta\right)\mathbbm{1}\left(H_{i,\mathcal{L}_{i}}^{L}\leq a_{i}\mathbf{1}\right)\mathbbm{1}\left(H_{i,\mathcal{U}_{i}}^{U}\geq b_{i}\mathbf{1}\right)\right].

Here, 𝒟obs\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}} denotes the observed data, and the inequalities inside the indicator functions are understood componentwise. The multivariate normal density is therefore evaluated for the full augmented latent vector at observed visits, while the indicator functions enforce the boundary constraints. This avoids the need for multivariate normal CDFs in model fitting, because the boundary probabilities are represented through constrained latent variables rather than analytically integrated out. Additional details on prior specification, covariance parameterization, and Stan implementation are given in Appendix A.

For later use in posterior predictive imputation, reorder the latent vector and mean vector so that observed visits precede missing visits, retaining increasing visit order within each block, and apply the same permutation to the rows and columns of the covariance matrix. With this reordering understood, write

Hi=(Hi,𝒪iHi,ℳi),μi​a=(μi​a,𝒪iμi​a,ℳi),Σa=(Σa,𝒪i​𝒪iΣa,𝒪i​ℳiΣa,ℳi​𝒪iΣa,ℳi​ℳi),H_{i}=\begin{pmatrix}H_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}}\\ H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mu_{ia}=\begin{pmatrix}\mu_{ia,\mathcal{O}_{i}}\\ \mu_{ia,\mathcal{M}_{i}}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Sigma_{a}=\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma_{a,\mathcal{O}_{i}\mathcal{O}_{i}}&\Sigma_{a,\mathcal{O}_{i}\mathcal{M}_{i}}\\ \Sigma_{a,\mathcal{M}_{i}\mathcal{O}_{i}}&\Sigma_{a,\mathcal{M}_{i}\mathcal{M}_{i}}\end{pmatrix}, (19)

where the observed latent subvector is represented by the augmented observed latent vector H~i,𝒪i\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}}. Under MAR within each arm, the conditional distribution of the missing outcomes on the latent working scale is Gaussian:

Hi,ℳi|H~i,𝒪i,Ai=a,Xi,θ∼𝒩(mi​aMAR(θ),Vi​aMAR(θ)),H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}}\left|\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}},A_{i}=a,X_{i},\theta\right.\sim\mathcal{N}\left(m_{ia}^{\mathrm{MAR}}\left(\theta\right),V_{ia}^{\mathrm{MAR}}\left(\theta\right)\right), (20)

where

mi​aMAR​(θ)=μi​a,ℳi+Σa,ℳi​𝒪i​Σa,𝒪i​𝒪i−1​(H~i,𝒪i−μi​a,𝒪i),m_{ia}^{\mathrm{MAR}}\left(\theta\right)=\mu_{ia,\mathcal{M}_{i}}+\Sigma_{a,\mathcal{M}_{i}\mathcal{O}_{i}}\Sigma_{a,\mathcal{O}_{i}\mathcal{O}_{i}}^{-1}\left(\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}}-\mu_{ia,\mathcal{O}_{i}}\right), (21)

and

Vi​aMAR​(θ)=Σa,ℳi​ℳi−Σa,ℳi​𝒪i​Σa,𝒪i​𝒪i−1​Σa,𝒪i​ℳi.V_{ia}^{\mathrm{MAR}}\left(\theta\right)=\Sigma_{a,\mathcal{M}_{i}\mathcal{M}_{i}}-\Sigma_{a,\mathcal{M}_{i}\mathcal{O}_{i}}\Sigma_{a,\mathcal{O}_{i}\mathcal{O}_{i}}^{-1}\Sigma_{a,\mathcal{O}_{i}\mathcal{M}_{i}}. (22)

Dependence of mi​aMAR​(θ)m_{ia}^{\mathrm{MAR}}\left(\theta\right) on the augmented observed latent vector is suppressed in the notation. The Gaussian conditional distribution applies for fixed model parameters and augmented boundary values; integrating over their posterior uncertainty generally yields a mixture of Gaussian distributions. When the conditioning visit set is empty, the corresponding conditional Gaussian distribution is interpreted as the marginal Gaussian distribution.

4.3 Reference-based sensitivity rules on the latent scale

The primary posterior under the arm-specific MAR model is learned from the augmented latent representation described above. The sensitivity rule enters only at the posterior predictive completion stage, through the distribution used to generate missing latent values in the active arm from the trigger onward.

Although the thresholded latent model permits bounds to vary across subjects and, in principle, covariance structures to differ between arms, we restrict attention to the case with a common covariance matrix, Σ0=Σ1=Σ\Sigma_{0}=\Sigma_{1}=\Sigma. This keeps the J2R and CR constructions on the latent scale aligned with the conventional Gaussian reference-based framework and yields a shared conditional covariance structure after the trigger, which underlies the variance invariance results presented later. Allowing Σ0≠Σ1\Sigma_{0}\neq\Sigma_{1} is conceptually possible but leads to more cumbersome conditioning formulas and is not pursued here.

For subject ii, let 𝒪i⋆=𝒪i∪ℳipre\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}=\mathcal{O}_{i}\cup\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}} denote the augmented conditioning set obtained after any missing latent values before the trigger have been imputed under the arm-specific MAR model. Under the final missing tail restriction, every visit in 𝒪i⋆\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star} precedes τi\tau_{i}, so the J2R conditioning formula below centers the entire augmented history at the active arm mean before the trigger. Then, H~i,𝒪i⋆\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}} denotes the realized latent history on that set, namely the augmented observed latent vector together with any latent values imputed for missing visits before the trigger, arranged in increasing order of visits, and the only components that remain to be generated under the sensitivity rule are those in ℳipost\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}. Dependence of the conditional means on the displayed conditioning history is suppressed in the notation.

Partition the arm-specific mean vector and the common covariance matrix according to the ordered index blocks (𝒪i⋆,ℳipost)\left(\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star},\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\right), so that

μi​a=(μi​a,𝒪i⋆μi​a,ℳipost),Σ=(Σ𝒪i⋆​𝒪i⋆Σ𝒪i⋆​ℳipostΣℳipost​𝒪i⋆Σℳipost​ℳipost).\mu_{ia}=\begin{pmatrix}\mu_{ia,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}\\ \mu_{ia,\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma_{\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}&\Sigma_{\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}\\ \Sigma_{\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}&\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}\end{pmatrix}. (23)

For a∈{0,1}a\in\left\{0,1\right\}, the MAR completion distribution in arm aa for missing latent values from the trigger onward is

Hi,ℳipost|H~i,𝒪i⋆,Ai=a,Xi,θ∼𝒩(mi​apost(θ),Vipost(θ)),H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}\left|\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}},A_{i}=a,X_{i},\theta\right.\sim\mathcal{N}\left(m_{ia}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right),V_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right)\right), (24)

where

mi​apost​(θ)=μi​a,ℳipost+Σℳipost​𝒪i⋆​Σ𝒪i⋆​𝒪i⋆−1​(H~i,𝒪i⋆−μi​a,𝒪i⋆),m_{ia}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right)=\mu_{ia,\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}+\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}\Sigma_{\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}^{-1}\left(\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}-\mu_{ia,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}\right), (25)

and

Vipost​(θ)=Σℳipost​ℳipost−Σℳipost​𝒪i⋆​Σ𝒪i⋆​𝒪i⋆−1​Σ𝒪i⋆​ℳipost.V_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right)=\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}-\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}\Sigma_{\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}^{-1}\Sigma_{\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}. (26)

Under MAR in the active arm, we take a=1a=1, so that

Hi,ℳipost|H~i,𝒪i⋆,Ai=1,Xi,θ∼𝒩(mi​1post(θ),Vipost(θ)).H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}\left|\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}},A_{i}=1,X_{i},\theta\right.\sim\mathcal{N}\left(m_{i1}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right),V_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right)\right). (27)

Under J2R, we construct the imputation distribution using a marginal latent mean trajectory that follows the active arm before the trigger and the reference arm afterward. Imputation is then conditional on the realized latent history. The completion distribution is

Hi,ℳipost|H~i,𝒪i⋆,Ai=1,Xi,θ∼𝒩(miJ2R(θ),Vipost(θ)),H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}\left|\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}},A_{i}=1,X_{i},\theta\right.\sim\mathcal{N}\left(m_{i}^{\mathrm{J2R}}\left(\theta\right),V_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right)\right), (28)

where

miJ2R​(θ)=μi​0,ℳipost+Σℳipost​𝒪i⋆​Σ𝒪i⋆​𝒪i⋆−1​(H~i,𝒪i⋆−μi​1,𝒪i⋆).m_{i}^{\mathrm{J2R}}\left(\theta\right)=\mu_{i0,\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}+\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}\Sigma_{\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}^{-1}\left(\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}-\mu_{i1,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}\right). (29)

Under CR, missing latent values in the active arm from the trigger onward are drawn from the same conditional distribution that would apply in the reference arm, given the realized augmented latent history:

Hi,ℳipost|H~i,𝒪i⋆,Ai=1,Xi,θ∼𝒩(miCR(θ),Vipost(θ)),H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}\left|\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}},A_{i}=1,X_{i},\theta\right.\sim\mathcal{N}\left(m_{i}^{\mathrm{CR}}\left(\theta\right),V_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right)\right), (30)

where

miCR​(θ)=μi​0,ℳipost+Σℳipost​𝒪i⋆​Σ𝒪i⋆​𝒪i⋆−1​(H~i,𝒪i⋆−μi​0,𝒪i⋆).m_{i}^{\mathrm{CR}}\left(\theta\right)=\mu_{i0,\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}+\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}\Sigma_{\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}^{-1}\left(\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}-\mu_{i0,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}\right). The formulation on the latent scale also admits a family of sensitivity rules that interpolates between MAR and J2R through a single parameter. Let ω∈[0,1]\omega\in\left[0,1\right] denote a prespecified sensitivity parameter, and define

ℓi,ωpost​(θ)=(1−ω)​mi​1post​(θ)+ω​miJ2R​(θ).\ell_{i,\omega}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right)=\left(1-\omega\right)m_{i1}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right)+\omega m_{i}^{\mathrm{J2R}}\left(\theta\right). (32)

We then use the completion distribution

Hi,ℳipost|H~i,𝒪i⋆,Ai=1,Xi,θ,ω∼𝒩(ℓi,ωpost(θ),Vipost(θ)).H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}\left|\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}},A_{i}=1,X_{i},\theta,\omega\right.\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\ell_{i,\omega}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right),V_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\theta\right)\right). (33)

This recovers ω=0\omega=0 as the MAR law for the active arm and ω=1\omega=1 as J2R, while intermediate values represent graded departures from MAR toward the reference arm trajectory.

4.4 Posterior predictive completion and estimation

The proposed method proceeds through posterior predictive completion on the latent working scale. Equivalently, for each chosen sensitivity rule, completion is based on the posterior predictive distribution obtained by averaging the corresponding conditional latent completion law over the fitted primary posterior. The primary model is first fitted under the arm-specific MAR assumption, yielding posterior draws

(θ(1),H~ℒ(1),H~𝒰(1)),…,(θ(K),H~ℒ(K),H~𝒰(K))\left(\theta^{\left(1\right)},\widetilde{H}_{\mathcal{L}}^{\left(1\right)},\widetilde{H}_{\mathcal{U}}^{\left(1\right)}\right),\dots,\left(\theta^{\left(K\right)},\widetilde{H}_{\mathcal{L}}^{\left(K\right)},\widetilde{H}_{\mathcal{U}}^{\left(K\right)}\right) (34)

from the primary posterior under the augmented latent representation, where H~ℒ(k)\widetilde{H}_{\mathcal{L}}^{\left(k\right)} and H~𝒰(k)\widetilde{H}_{\mathcal{U}}^{\left(k\right)} denote the collections of augmented latent values corresponding to observed outcomes at the lower and upper bounds in posterior draw kk. All model quantities and augmented observed boundary values in the completion formulas are evaluated at posterior draw kk; the draw index is suppressed where unambiguous. For each retained posterior draw, missing latent outcomes are then completed under the arm-specific MAR law before the trigger time and under the chosen reference-based rule after the trigger in the active arm.

For posterior draw θ(k)\theta^{\left(k\right)}, with k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K, completion proceeds subject by subject. If ℳipre≠∅\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}\neq\varnothing, the missing latent values before the trigger are first sampled under the arm-specific MAR law:

Hi,ℳipre|H~i,𝒪i,Ai,Xi,θ(k)∼𝒩(mi​Aipre(θ(k)),Vipre(θ(k))),H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}}\left|\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}},A_{i},X_{i},\theta^{\left(k\right)}\right.\sim\mathcal{N}\left(m_{iA_{i}}^{\mathrm{pre}}\left(\theta^{\left(k\right)}\right),V_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}\left(\theta^{\left(k\right)}\right)\right), (35)

where

mi​Aipre​(θ(k))=μi​Ai,ℳipre+ΣAi,ℳipre​𝒪i​ΣAi,𝒪i​𝒪i−1​(H~i,𝒪i−μi​Ai,𝒪i),m_{iA_{i}}^{\mathrm{pre}}\left(\theta^{\left(k\right)}\right)=\mu_{iA_{i},\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}}+\Sigma_{A_{i},\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}\mathcal{O}_{i}}\Sigma_{A_{i},\mathcal{O}_{i}\mathcal{O}_{i}}^{-1}\left(\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}}-\mu_{iA_{i},\mathcal{O}_{i}}\right), (36)

and

Vipre​(θ(k))=ΣAi,ℳipre​ℳipre−ΣAi,ℳipre​𝒪i​ΣAi,𝒪i​𝒪i−1​ΣAi,𝒪i​ℳipre.V_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}\left(\theta^{\left(k\right)}\right)=\Sigma_{A_{i},\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}}-\Sigma_{A_{i},\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}\mathcal{O}_{i}}\Sigma_{A_{i},\mathcal{O}_{i}\mathcal{O}_{i}}^{-1}\Sigma_{A_{i},\mathcal{O}_{i}\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}}. (37)

These draws are combined with the observed latent history to form the augmented conditioning set 𝒪i⋆=𝒪i∪ℳipre\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}=\mathcal{O}_{i}\cup\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{pre}}. Conditional on H~i,𝒪i⋆\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}, the missing latent values from the trigger onward are then completed. If ℳipost=∅\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}=\varnothing, no further completion is required. Otherwise, the remaining missing latent values are generated under the arm-specific MAR law for subjects in the reference arm and under the chosen reference-based completion rule for subjects in the active arm.

After all missing latent values have been obtained, the completed latent vector

Hi(k)=(Hi​1(k),…,Hi​T(k))⊤H_{i}^{\left(k\right)}=\left(H_{i1}^{\left(k\right)},\dots,H_{iT}^{\left(k\right)}\right)^{\top} (38)

is mapped back to the observed outcome scale through the thresholded observation rule

Yi​t(k)={Li,if ​Hi​t(k)≤ai,Li+(Ui−Li)​Φ⁡(Hi​t(k))−pLipUi−pLi,if ​ai<Hi​t(k)<bi,Ui,if ​Hi​t(k)≥bi.Y_{it}^{\left(k\right)}=\begin{cases}L_{i},&\text{if }H_{it}^{\left(k\right)}\leq a_{i},\\ L_{i}+\left(U_{i}-L_{i}\right)\dfrac{\Phi\left(H_{it}^{\left(k\right)}\right)-p_{L_{i}}}{p_{U_{i}}-p_{L_{i}}},&\text{if }a_{i}<H_{it}^{\left(k\right)}<b_{i},\\ U_{i},&\text{if }H_{it}^{\left(k\right)}\geq b_{i}.\end{cases} (39)

Because this rule is defined on all of ℝ\mathbb{R}, each draw of a completed dataset automatically respects the required support restriction and may contain values exactly at the lower or upper bound whenever the latent draws fall outside the interior interval (ai,bi)\left(a_{i},b_{i}\right).

Inference may target a quantity defined for the completed study cohort. For retained posterior draw k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K, let Y(k)={Yi​t(k):i=1,…,n,t=1,…,T}Y^{\left(k\right)}=\left\{Y_{it}^{\left(k\right)}:i=1,\dots,n,\;t=1,\dots,T\right\} denote the completed outcome data on the original scale. Let Q⁡(⋅,A,X)Q\left(\,\cdot\,,A,X\right) denote such a quantity, for example, an arm mean or a contrast between arm means, and define Q(k)=Q⁡(Y(k),A,X)Q^{\left(k\right)}=Q\left(Y^{\left(k\right)},A,X\right), where A=(A1,…,An)A=\left(A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\right) denotes the treatment assignments and XX the collection of covariates for all subjects and visits.

Posterior predictive summaries of quantities defined for the completed study cohort are obtained directly from Q(1),…,Q(K)Q^{\left(1\right)},\dots,Q^{\left(K\right)} and describe uncertainty about those quantities conditional on the observed data. Population treatment effect inference additionally requires accounting for uncertainty about the treatment effect given a completed dataset. When using a secondary analysis model for this purpose, let MM denote the number of completed datasets used for that analysis. The secondary model is fitted to each completed dataset, and the resulting point estimates and within-imputation variance estimates are combined using Rubin’s rules (Rubin,, 1987). Thus, KK denotes the number of retained post-warmup posterior draws used for direct posterior predictive summaries, whereas MM denotes the number of completed datasets used for the secondary analysis.

An important theoretical feature of the proposed construction is variance invariance on the latent scale for the class of post-trigger rules considered here. Conditional on the fitted posterior state, MAR, J2R, CR, and the ω\omega-weighted rules modify only the conditional mean of the vector of missing latent values from the trigger onward and leave its conditional covariance unchanged. This yields an exact conditional variance invariance result for estimands that are affine functions of the completed data on the latent scale. On the observed bounded scale, because the threshold map is nonlinear and is not differentiable at the latent thresholds, we provide only a local first-order heuristic under the conditions stated in Appendix B, rather than a full theorem on information anchoring on the observed scale. Formal statements, proofs, and the heuristic on the observed scale are given in Appendix B. The result pertains to affine estimands computed directly from the completed latent data. It does not, in general, imply exact variance invariance for secondary analyses fitted to the completed datasets on the observed scale and then combined using multiple imputation rules.

5 Simulation studies

We conducted three complementary simulation studies. Study 1 examined calibration of the bounded outcome working models under incomplete follow-up, and Study 2 assessed recovery of the complete data contrast in each replicate under alternative assumptions after the trigger. Study 3 evaluated population treatment effect inference using imputation followed by a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) on the observed scale and Rubin’s rules, including a transformed Gaussian comparator and a targeted distributional misspecification scenario.

All three studies used outcomes bounded by [0,63]\left[0,63\right] and the half-step thresholds defined using unit score step s=1s=1. Studies 1 and 2 used 50 subjects randomized equally between arms and five post-baseline visits. Study 3 used 100 subjects randomized equally between arms and four post-baseline visits.

In Studies 1 and 2, 300 replicates were attempted per scenario; computational failures were excluded, leaving 297 to 300 replicates per scenario and model in Study 1 and 298 to 300 per scenario in Study 2. Study 3 summaries used 300 replicates per scenario. Study 2 assessed recovery of the contrast between arm means in the complete data for each replicate. Study 3 assessed inference for a fixed population treatment effect by fitting an MMRM to each completed dataset and combining the treatment effect estimates and their variance estimates using Rubin’s rules. Exact simulation inputs and supplementary results are provided in Web Appendix B of the Supporting Information.

5.1 Primary model calibration under incomplete follow-up

Study 1 was designed to benchmark three working models: a Gaussian model for repeated measures fitted directly on the observed scale, a bounded working model based on a continuous interior transformation without explicit boundary mass, and the proposed mixed-boundary model. We report the summaries most directly tied to calibration of the proposed mixed-boundary formulation.

The four scenarios for data generation were chosen to span a progression from mild to substantial boundary accumulation. Rather than selecting latent means and variances ad hoc, we specified, at each visit, the probabilities of the lower and upper bounds in the control arm on the observed scale, together with a visit-specific standardized treatment shift and an AR(1) correlation parameter. The corresponding latent intercepts and marginal latent SDs were then obtained analytically so that the thresholded latent Gaussian generator reproduced the chosen control arm boundary probabilities exactly. This makes the scenario definitions interpretable on the observed scale while keeping data generation fully aligned with the fitted latent model. The exact inputs are reported in Web Table 1.

After generating complete data, we imposed monotone dropout with a hazard that depended only on visit. This missingness mechanism was a special case of MAR. Study 1 was therefore not intended to assess sensitivity analysis assumptions. Its purpose was to assess whether the proposed mixed-boundary model remained well calibrated under realistically incomplete follow-up. The resulting mean missingness pattern by scenario and visit is summarized in Web Table 2.

The reported Study 1 summaries include recovery of the latent intercepts, latent treatment effects, and implied probabilities of the lower and upper bounds at each visit under the proposed mixed-boundary model, together with recovery of arm means on the observed scale across all three working models. These summaries are reported in Web Table 3, Web Table 4, Web Table 5, Web Table 6, and Web Table 7.

Posterior mean estimates of boundary probabilities showed upward bias. Empirical interval coverage was generally close to nominal, although some settings showed undercoverage.

Differences among the working models were modest in the milder settings. Under AggressiveCeiling, the mixed-boundary model showed smaller absolute bias and coverage closer to nominal than the continuous bounded model for the means in both arms on the observed scale at the final visit. However, performance depended on the scenario, arm, and summary measure; the Gaussian model was not uniformly inferior.

5.2 Operating characteristics of the reference-based sensitivity analyses

Study 2 used the same thresholded latent Gaussian generator but shifted the focus from calibration of the model for the observed data to the distribution of missing outcomes after the trigger. The design crossed two support templates with four truth rules for the active arm after the trigger, yielding eight scenarios in total. The first support template, ModerateFloor, represents increasing accumulation at the lower bound with little mass at the upper bound. The second, AggressiveBothBounds, represents a deliberately more challenging two-sided boundary setting. Within each support template, the truth in the active arm after the trigger was taken to follow MAR, a weighted J2R rule with ω=0.50\omega=0.50, J2R, or CR. This factorial construction separates the support structure from the truth rule after the trigger and makes clear how the final scenario set was obtained. The exact template specifications and combinations of truth rules are listed in Web Table 8.

Missingness was introduced through a mechanism for loss to follow-up comprising intermittent gaps before a final monotone missing tail. For each subject, the trigger time was defined pragmatically as the visit immediately after the last observed post-baseline outcome. Missing values before the trigger were generated under MAR within each arm, whereas values in the final missing tail in the active arm followed the truth rule for that scenario. The resulting mean missingness pattern is summarized in Web Table 9.

Each dataset in Study 2 was analyzed only with the proposed mixed-boundary model, holding the fitted model fixed across sensitivity analyses. The analysis rules were MAR, weighted J2R with ω=0.50\omega=0.50, J2R, and CR. The target in each replicate was the difference between the sample means in the active and reference arms at the final scheduled visit on the observed bounded scale. For each replicate, this true contrast was calculated from the complete outcomes generated under the scenario’s truth rule, before masking the missing values. It therefore varied across replicates within a scenario. For each analysis rule, we generated one posterior predictive completed dataset per retained post-warmup draw and calculated the corresponding sample contrast. No secondary model was fitted on the observed scale, and no Rubin combination was used.

Bias was the average difference between the posterior mean contrast and the true contrast for that replicate. RMSE was the square root of the average squared difference, and coverage was the proportion of central 95%95\% posterior intervals containing the corresponding true contrast. These summaries assess recovery of the realized complete data contrast rather than inference for a fixed population treatment effect.

Absolute bias was smallest under the matching analysis rule in seven of the eight scenarios, whereas RMSE did not consistently favor the matching rule. The mean contrast estimates under weighted J2R generally lay between those under MAR and J2R. The retained numerical summary is reported in Web Table 10.

5.3 Population treatment effect inference after multiple imputation

Study 3 evaluated the application’s procedure: imputation followed by MMRM analysis and pooling using Rubin’s rules. Four scenarios crossed two latent error distributions (Gaussian and heavy-tailed multivariate Student tt with five degrees of freedom, denoted t5t_{5}) with MAR or J2R truth after the trigger. Each replicate included 100 subjects, four post-baseline outcomes, and a fully observed prognostic baseline covariate. Missingness combined intermittent gaps and a final missing tail, with approximately 39.5%39.5\% missing at the final visit. The target was the fixed population mean difference, active minus reference, on the observed scale at that visit, integrating over the baseline covariate and missingness patterns. Detailed design and computational settings appear in Web Section B.4.

We compared mixed-boundary imputation with a Gaussian model for log⁡(1+Y)\log\left(1+Y\right), where YY is the simulated outcome on the original scale. The latter model’s imputations were back-transformed and clipped to [0,63]\left[0,63\right]. Both imputation models and the observed-scale MMRM used visit-specific intercepts, baseline effects, and treatment effects, with an unstructured covariance matrix common to both arms. Each imputation model supplied 4,000 completed datasets per rule under MAR, J2R, CR, and WJ2R(0.50), using all post-warmup draws. This increased the application’s 50 imputations per rule to reduce imputation Monte Carlo variability while retaining its analysis and pooling procedure: MMRM analysis of each completed dataset and combination of treatment contrasts using Rubin’s rules. The same MMRM fitted before masking outcomes provided a complete-data benchmark. Performance measures were bias, empirical SD, mean estimated standard error (SE), and coverage of nominal 95%95\% intervals.

When the analysis and truth rules matched, the mixed-boundary model showed small bias under both error distributions, including the heavy-tailed scenarios where its Gaussian working distribution was misspecified (Table 1). Its absolute bias was smaller than the shifted-log comparator’s under MAR truth and similar under J2R truth. The comparator had slightly smaller empirical SDs, so neither method was uniformly superior.

Rubin’s variance quantifies uncertainty about the fixed population contrast, whereas the empirical SD measures sampling variability of the pooled estimator. Both methods produced conservative J2R intervals, with mean Rubin SEs exceeding empirical SDs. This can arise because Rubin’s variance estimator need not equal the pooled estimator’s repeated-sampling variance under reference-based imputation (Bartlett,, 2023). This assessment is distinct from the latent-scale conditional variance result in Appendix B.

Results for all sensitivity rules appear in Web Table 11. Rules differing from the generating truth describe sensitivity to assumptions about missing outcomes and are not expected to yield nominal coverage.

6 Application

We reanalyzed the 97 retained BtheB subjects to estimate differences between BtheB and TAU in mean BDI-II at each post-baseline visit, adjusting for baseline. We focused on the final assessment at 8 months; negative contrasts favor BtheB. MAR served as the baseline analysis, with reference-based rules assessing sensitivity to assumptions about missing data after the trigger. As intercurrent event information was unavailable, the trigger was defined from the follow-up pattern, without assigning a hypothetical or treatment policy interpretation.

There were T=4T=4 post-baseline visits, with visit TT corresponding to the 8-month assessment. For subject ii, let tilastt_{i}^{\mathrm{last}} denote the last post-baseline visit at which BDI-II was observed. If tilast<Tt_{i}^{\mathrm{last}}<T, we set τi=tilast+1\tau_{i}=t_{i}^{\mathrm{last}}+1, so that the set of missing visits from the trigger onward corresponds to the final monotone missing tail after the last observed post-baseline value. If the final scheduled visit was observed, we set τi=T+1\tau_{i}=T+1, and no sensitivity rule was applied.

TAU was the reference arm. Missing outcomes in TAU were imputed under MAR. For the final missing tail in BtheB, MAR retained the active arm predictive distribution, whereas J2R, CR, and WJ2R(0.50) modified the latent conditional mean according to the rules in Section 4.

The mixed-boundary imputation model used the thresholded latent Gaussian formulation from Section 4. On the latent scale, the visit-specific linear predictor was

μi​t=αt+βtbase​BDIi,base+Ai​δt,\mu_{it}=\alpha_{t}+\beta_{t}^{\mathrm{base}}\,\text{BDI}_{i,\mathrm{base}}+A_{i}\delta_{t}, (40)

where BDIi,base\text{BDI}_{i,\mathrm{base}} denotes centered baseline BDI-II, αt\alpha_{t} is the visit-specific intercept, βtbase\beta_{t}^{\mathrm{base}} is the visit-specific baseline effect, δt\delta_{t} is the visit-specific treatment effect, and AiA_{i} is the randomized treatment indicator, with Ai=1A_{i}=1 for BtheB and Ai=0A_{i}=0 for TAU.

6.1 Predictive model comparison

We compared the Gaussian, continuous bounded, and mixed-boundary working models using leave-one-subject-out prediction. To place the comparison on a common scale, each model was scored using the joint probability of the intervals [y−0.5,y+0.5)\left[y-0.5,y+0.5\right) across a subject’s observed visits. This avoids comparing boundary probability masses directly with continuous densities. Predictive probabilities were estimated using Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS), with explicit refits when its diagnostics were inadequate (Vehtari et al.,, 2017; Vehtari et al.,, 2025; Vehtari et al.,, 2024). Appendix C defines the comparison, and Web Appendix C of the Supporting Information gives computational details.

The continuous bounded model had the highest expected log predictive density (ELPD), with a modest advantage over the mixed-boundary model (Table 2). The mixed-boundary minus continuous bounded difference was −3.89-3.89 (SE 2.102.10). Both bounded models had higher ELPD than the Gaussian model; the mixed-boundary minus Gaussian difference was 24.1824.18 (SE 15.0015.00). These SEs account for pairing by subject.

We also compared predictions under MAR for subjects with missing BDI-II at month 8 (see Web Table 12 in Web Appendix D of the Supporting Information). The mixed-boundary model assigned positive probability to imputations equal to zero and higher probability to the common interval [−0.5,0.5)\left[-0.5,0.5\right), representing scores that round to zero. For this interval, its predicted probabilities exceeded those of the continuous bounded model by 3.45 percentage points in TAU and 3.77 in BtheB. These differences describe the consequences of model choice, without establishing which model predicts the missing outcomes more accurately.

6.2 Sensitivity analyses

For the reference-based sensitivity analyses, we used the mixed-boundary model to obtain imputations within the known support that may equal the bounds exactly. The predictive comparison assesses observed outcomes and does not validate the assumptions about missing outcomes after the trigger.

For each completed dataset, we estimated the treatment contrasts on the observed scale using an MMRM with visit-specific intercepts, baseline BDI-II effects, and treatment effects, fitted by restricted maximum likelihood with a common unstructured covariance matrix across treatment arms. The model was fitted using nlme::gls (Pinheiro et al.,, 2025), with corSymm for the correlations and varIdent for variances that differ across visits. Let M=50M=50 denote the number of completed datasets used for this downstream multiple imputation analysis. Under each rule, we generated MM posterior predictive completed datasets from the fitted mixed-boundary model, fitted an MMRM to each completed dataset, and combined the resulting visit-specific treatment contrasts using Rubin’s rules (Rubin,, 1987). Figure 4 shows negative treatment contrasts under all four rules at every visit. At 8 months, CR gave the most negative estimate and MAR the least negative, with substantial overlap between the corresponding 95% intervals. Thus, the sensitivity assumptions affected the estimated magnitude but did not reverse the direction favoring BtheB, consistent with the original trial. These shifts in point estimates are distinct from interval calibration, which was assessed separately in Study 3. At 8 months, all four 95% intervals included zero, so none of the sensitivity rules yielded a statistically significant treatment contrast.

To interpret the sensitivity rules on the observed scale, Figure 5 displays mean BDI-II and the probability of a score of exactly zero, including the TAU reference profiles. Under each rule, we generated one completed dataset per retained posterior draw (K=4000K=4000), keeping observed outcomes fixed, and calculated the mean and proportion of zeros within each arm at each visit. Points show posterior means; interval limits are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. These intervals describe uncertainty in the completed cohort summaries, separately from the MMRM and Rubin analysis. Differences between the completed cohort arm means need not equal the MMRM treatment contrasts, which adjust for baseline BDI-II.

The profiles in Figure 5 show that, at 5 and 8 months, CR yielded lower mean BDI-II and higher zero probabilities than the other BtheB rules. J2R did not make the completed BtheB profiles coincide with TAU: the rules apply to missing outcomes conditional on individual histories, while the profiles also reflect retained observations and covariate differences between arms. Moreover, the nonlinear threshold map means that weighting the latent means does not generally produce the same weighting of observed means or boundary probabilities. Here, the WJ2R(0.50) profiles were close to the midpoints of MAR and J2R.

The alternative threshold specifications examined produced little change in the completed cohort means and probabilities of zero at month 8 (Web Table 13).

7 Discussion

This paper extends familiar reference-based sensitivity analysis to bounded longitudinal outcomes by placing the sensitivity assumption on a latent Gaussian working scale and mapping completed values back to the original bounded scale. The resulting framework respects the known support by construction, allows exact boundary values to arise naturally, and retains the conditional Gaussian completion machinery that makes reference-based methods operationally attractive.

The proposed thresholded latent Gaussian model is related to Tobit and coarsening models, which represent boundary observations through latent regions (Xu et al.,, 2014). Reference-based imputation using a Tobit model has also been studied for censored survival outcomes (Atkinson et al.,, 2021). Here, boundary scores are valid outcomes, and the latent representation does not imply scores beyond the bounds.

Studies 1 and 2 assessed model calibration and recovery of realized complete data contrasts. Study 3 separately evaluated population treatment effect inference after imputation and found small bias when the analysis rule matched the truth rule after the trigger, but conservative Rubin intervals, particularly under J2R. Similar conservatism occurred with the shifted-log comparator. The heavy-tailed scenario provides a limited assessment of distributional robustness; it does not establish robustness to other forms of misspecification. These findings also emphasize that conditional variance invariance on the latent scale does not guarantee nominal frequentist coverage for the downstream MMRM and Rubin procedure. In the BtheB application, the estimated treatment contrasts were broadly stable across sensitivity assumptions, although differences at later visits showed the expected dependence on the assumed distribution of missing outcomes after the trigger.

The comparison using common score intervals showed a modest predictive advantage for the continuous bounded model over the mixed-boundary model. The separate comparison for missing outcomes showed that model choice also affected predictions near zero, although these differences do not establish which model better represents the unobserved outcomes.

The framework links boundary probabilities and the interior distribution through a latent Gaussian model with fixed thresholds. A separate process generating boundary outcomes may require a more flexible model. The current development assumes a common latent covariance matrix across arms. Implementation requires MCMC sampling and convergence checks, adding computational effort and requiring familiarity with Bayesian model fitting. The sensitivity assumptions also require interpretation on the observed scale and cannot be verified from the observed data alone. Future work could examine practical guidance for choosing threshold locations, study performance more systematically under sparse versus substantial boundary mass, relax the assumption of a common covariance matrix, and extend the framework to ordinal, semicontinuous, and other coarsened bounded outcomes.

Appendix

Appendix A Stan implementation of the primary model

The primary model was fitted in Stan by sampling from the augmented posterior described in Section 4. In the current implementation, observed interior outcomes enter through their deterministic latent transforms, whereas observed outcomes at the lower and upper bounds are represented by constrained latent variables. Thus, posterior sampling proceeds directly under the augmented latent Gaussian representation, without requiring multivariate normal rectangle probabilities in the fitting step.

In the current implementation, we adopt the formulation with a common covariance matrix described in Section 4, so that Σ0=Σ1=Σ\Sigma_{0}=\Sigma_{1}=\Sigma. The covariance matrix is parameterized through marginal latent SDs and a correlation matrix:

Σ=diag⁡(σ1,…,σT)​R​diag⁡(σ1,…,σT),\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{T}\right)R\operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{T}\right), (41)

where RR is a T×TT\times T correlation matrix. In Stan, RR is represented through its Cholesky factor LRL_{R}, and we write

LΣ=diag⁡(σ1,…,σT)​LR,Σ=LΣ​LΣ⊤.L_{\Sigma}=\operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{T}\right)L_{R},\qquad\Sigma=L_{\Sigma}L_{\Sigma}^{\top}. (42)

This Cholesky parameterization improves numerical stability and sampling efficiency.

We used the following proper prior distributions. For the visit-specific coefficient vectors entering the mean specification

μi​a​t=Xi​t⊤βt+aWi​t⊤δt,t=1,…,T,\mu_{iat}=X_{it}^{\top}\beta_{t}+aW_{it}^{\top}\delta_{t},\qquad t=1,\dots,T, (43)

we used independent normal priors centered at zero, which may be written as

βt,δt∼𝒩⁡(0,1002​I),\beta_{t},\delta_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,100^{2}I\right), (44)

with identity matrices of conformable dimension.

For the marginal latent SDs, we used independent half-tt priors with 33 degrees of freedom, location 00, and scale 1010,

σt∼t3+(0,10),t=1,…,T.\sigma_{t}\sim t_{3}^{+}\left(0,10\right),\qquad t=1,\dots,T. (45)

This specification uses the half-tt prior family for positive scale parameters discussed by Gelman, (2006). For the correlation matrix, we used the Lewandowski-Kurowicka-Joe (LKJ) prior with shape parameter 11, R∼LKJ⁡(1)R\sim\mathrm{LKJ}\left(1\right), which is uniform over correlation matrices (Lewandowski et al.,, 2009). Posterior computation was carried out in Stan (Carpenter et al.,, 2017) using the No-U-Turn Sampler, an adaptive form of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Hoffman and Gelman,, 2014). The number of post-warmup draws and completed datasets used for each analysis are specified in the corresponding sections.

Appendix B Variance invariance in the latent threshold model

Following Cro et al., (2019), an information-anchored sensitivity analysis preserves the proportion of information about the treatment estimand that is lost due to missing data when moving from the primary analysis to the sensitivity analysis. Theoretical results on information anchoring are available for controlled multiple imputation and RBMI with longitudinal continuous outcomes (Cro et al.,, 2019) and for reference-based sensitivity analysis under imputation models based on truncated normal distributions or Tobit formulations (Atkinson et al.,, 2021). For the proposed thresholded model for bounded outcomes with discrete and continuous components, we do not establish a full theorem on information anchoring on the observed scale. Instead, we establish exact conditional variance invariance on the latent scale for post-trigger rules that share the same slope matrix for the conditioning history and the same conditional covariance, while allowing the conditional mean intercept to differ. Under the common covariance formulation, this class includes MAR, J2R, CR, and the ω\omega-weighted rules considered in Section 4. For quantities that are affine functions of the completed data on the latent scale, this yields exact conditional variance invariance. On the observed bounded scale, the threshold map is nonlinear and is not differentiable at the latent thresholds, so we provide only a local first-order heuristic under the conditions stated below.

Throughout this appendix, let ϑ\vartheta denote the full posterior state under the primary model, consisting of the structural parameters together with any augmented latent variables introduced for observed boundary values. Conditional on ϑ\vartheta and the observed data 𝒟obs\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}, the sensitivity analysis enters only through the posterior predictive distribution of the missing latent outcomes from the trigger onward; it does not alter the posterior distribution p⁡(ϑ|𝒟obs)p\left(\vartheta\middle|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right). We write rr for a generic post-trigger sensitivity rule. In this appendix, the rule rr is assumed to belong to the class

Hi,ℳipost(r)|H~i,𝒪i⋆,Ai=1,Xi,ϑ∼𝒩(mi(r)(ϑ),Vipost(ϑ)),H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}}^{\left(r\right)}\left|\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}},A_{i}=1,X_{i},\vartheta\right.\sim\mathcal{N}\left(m_{i}^{\left(r\right)}\left(\vartheta\right),V_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\vartheta\right)\right), (46)

with

mi(r)​(ϑ)=ci(r)​(ϑ)+Bi​(ϑ)​H~i,𝒪i⋆,m_{i}^{\left(r\right)}\left(\vartheta\right)=c_{i}^{\left(r\right)}\left(\vartheta\right)+B_{i}\left(\vartheta\right)\widetilde{H}_{i,\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}, (47)

and

Bi​(ϑ)=Σℳipost​𝒪i⋆​Σ𝒪i⋆​𝒪i⋆−1.B_{i}\left(\vartheta\right)=\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}\Sigma_{\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\star}}^{-1}. (48)

That is, the rules considered here may change the intercept term ci(r)​(ϑ)c_{i}^{\left(r\right)}\left(\vartheta\right), but they share the same slope matrix Bi​(ϑ)B_{i}\left(\vartheta\right) and the same conditional covariance Vipost​(ϑ)V_{i}^{\mathrm{post}}\left(\vartheta\right). Under the formulation with a common covariance matrix described in Section 4, this class includes MAR, J2R, CR, and the ω\omega-weighted rules introduced there.

both of which are free of rr. Combining the covariance blocks yields the stated matrix. ∎

Proposition 2.

Let QH(r)=q0(r)​(ϑ,𝒟obs)+∑i=1ndi⊤​Hi,ℳi(r)Q_{H}^{\left(r\right)}=q_{0}^{\left(r\right)}\left(\vartheta,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i}^{\top}H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}}^{\left(r\right)} be any estimand that is an affine function of the completed data on the latent scale, where the vectors did_{i} do not depend on the post-trigger rule. Proof.

Conditional on ϑ\vartheta and 𝒟obs\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}, the only random components in QH(r)Q_{H}^{\left(r\right)} are the missing latent vectors Hi,ℳi(r)H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}}^{\left(r\right)}, and these vectors are independent across subjects under the model. Hence

Var(QH(r)|ϑ,𝒟obs)=∑i=1ndi⊤Cov(Hi,ℳi(r)|ϑ,𝒟obs)di.\mathrm{Var}\left(Q_{H}^{\left(r\right)}\middle|\vartheta,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i}^{\top}\mathrm{Cov}\left(H_{i,\mathcal{M}_{i}}^{\left(r\right)}\middle|\vartheta,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right)d_{i}. (58)

The result now follows immediately from Proposition 1. ∎

Proposition 2gives an exact conditional variance invariance result on the latent scale for the class of rules considered here. Conditional on the fitted posterior state, the post-trigger sensitivity rule changes only the location of the missing latent Gaussian distribution and does not change its covariance. Thus, for estimands that are affine functions of the completed data on the latent scale, the conditional contribution of missing data to the variance is preserved across sensitivity analyses.

B.2 Posterior integration and variation across posterior states

Assume that the completed-data quantities considered below have finite second moments under their posterior predictive distributions.

For any estimand that is an affine function of the completed data on the latent scale, QH(r)Q_{H}^{\left(r\right)}, the law of total variance gives

Var(QH(r)|𝒟obs)=E[Var(QH(r)|ϑ,𝒟obs)|𝒟obs]+Var(E[QH(r)|ϑ,𝒟obs]|𝒟obs).\mathrm{Var}\left(Q_{H}^{\left(r\right)}\middle|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right)=E\left[\mathrm{Var}\left(Q_{H}^{\left(r\right)}\middle|\vartheta,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right)\middle|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right]+\mathrm{Var}\left(E\left[Q_{H}^{\left(r\right)}\middle|\vartheta,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right]\middle|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right). (59)

By Proposition 2, the first term is identical across all rules rr in the class above. Therefore, any difference between rules in the posterior variance conditional on 𝒟obs\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}} must arise entirely through the second term, namely variation in the conditional mean across posterior states.

More precisely, for any two rules rr and r′r^{\prime}, exact equality of Var⁡(QH(r)|𝒟obs)\mathrm{Var}\left(Q_{H}^{\left(r\right)}\middle|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right) and Var⁡(QH(r′)|𝒟obs)\mathrm{Var}\left(Q_{H}^{\left(r^{\prime}\right)}\middle|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right) continues to hold whenever the difference E[QH(r)|ϑ,𝒟obs]−E[QH(r′)|ϑ,𝒟obs]E\left[Q_{H}^{\left(r\right)}\middle|\vartheta,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right]-E\left[Q_{H}^{\left(r^{\prime}\right)}\middle|\vartheta,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right] is constant in ϑ\vartheta. This covers the special case in which the rule changes the conditional mean only by an additive constant that does not depend on the posterior state. Otherwise, any remaining discrepancy reflects variation across posterior states rather than a change in the conditional covariance of the missing data.

B.3 A first-order heuristic on the observed scale

Let QY(r)=ψ⁡(Ycomp,(r),A,X)Q_{Y}^{\left(r\right)}=\psi\left(Y^{\mathrm{comp},\left(r\right)},A,X\right) denote an estimand evaluated on the completed data on the observed scale. Let Hℳ(r)H_{\mathcal{M}}^{\left(r\right)} denote the stacked missing latent vector under rule rr, arranged in a fixed order across subjects and visits. Write G⁡(h)G\left(h\right) for the componentwise threshold map that sends a candidate missing latent vector hh to the corresponding vector of completed missing observed outcomes under the thresholded observation rule in Section 4.1. Let Ycomp​(h)Y^{\mathrm{comp}}\left(h\right) denote the full completed observed outcome vector obtained by combining the observed outcomes YobsY_{\mathrm{obs}} with the missing observed outcomes G⁡(h)G\left(h\right). Define F⁡(h)=ψ⁡(Ycomp​(h),A,X)F\left(h\right)=\psi\left(Y^{\mathrm{comp}}\left(h\right),A,X\right). For a fixed posterior state ϑ\vartheta, let mr(ϑ)=E[Hℳ(r)|ϑ,𝒟obs]m_{r}\left(\vartheta\right)=E\left[H_{\mathcal{M}}^{\left(r\right)}\middle|\vartheta,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right] and Σℳ(ϑ)=Cov(Hℳ(r)|ϑ,𝒟obs)\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}}\left(\vartheta\right)=\mathrm{Cov}\left(H_{\mathcal{M}}^{\left(r\right)}\middle|\vartheta,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right), where Proposition 1 implies that Σℳ​(ϑ)\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}}\left(\vartheta\right) is common across rules in the class above.

The map GG is piecewise smooth but is not differentiable at the thresholds. Accordingly, the following argument is only local. For each rule being compared, suppose that there exists a neighborhood of mr​(ϑ)m_{r}\left(\vartheta\right) on which FF is continuously differentiable and that the conditional distribution of Hℳ(r)H_{\mathcal{M}}^{\left(r\right)} places negligible mass outside that neighborhood. In addition, assume that the first-order Taylor remainder contributes negligibly to the conditional variance, including through its covariance with the linear term. This assumption concerns both curvature within the neighborhood and contributions from draws outside it, including threshold crossings. Under these conditions, a first-order approximation using the delta method gives

Var(QY(r)|ϑ,𝒟obs)≈∇F(mr(ϑ))⊤Σℳ(ϑ)∇F(mr(ϑ)).\mathrm{Var}\left(Q_{Y}^{\left(r\right)}\middle|\vartheta,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{obs}}\right)\approx\nabla F\left(m_{r}\left(\vartheta\right)\right)^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathcal{M}}\left(\vartheta\right)\nabla F\left(m_{r}\left(\vartheta\right)\right). (60)

Accordingly, approximate conditional variance invariance on the observed scale is plausible when the local linear approximations are adequate, the gradients ∇F​(mr​(ϑ))\nabla F\left(m_{r}\left(\vartheta\right)\right) are similar across rules, and the rules do not move appreciable latent probability mass across the thresholds. Smoothness away from the thresholds alone does not ensure similar variances.

This is a heuristic rather than an exact theorem. A rigorous justification of the variance approximation would require quantitative control of the Taylor remainder, including contributions from threshold crossings and the atoms at the bounds. Approximate variance invariance would additionally require control of differences between the gradients across rules. We do not develop those bounds here.

Appendix C Predictive comparison on a common score scale

C.1 Common score intervals

The mixed-boundary model has a continuous interior density and probability masses at the bounds, whereas the Gaussian and continuous bounded models have continuous densities. Direct comparison of these native predictive ordinates would mix different measures at the bounds. We therefore evaluated all three models through probabilities of the same score intervals. The original likelihoods and priors were retained for fitting; the interval convention was used only for predictive evaluation.

For an integer BDI-II score yy, define I(y)=[y−0.5,y+0.5)I\left(y\right)=\left[y-0.5,y+0.5\right). For model mm, let θm\theta_{m} denote its structural parameters and define

qi​m(θm)=Prm(Yi​trep∈I(yi​t) for every t∈𝒪i|Ai,Xi,θm),q_{im}\left(\theta_{m}\right)=\Pr_{m}\left(Y_{it}^{\mathrm{rep}}\in I\left(y_{it}\right)\text{ for every }t\in\mathcal{O}_{i}\middle|A_{i},X_{i},\theta_{m}\right), (61)

where YirepY_{i}^{\mathrm{rep}} is a new outcome vector with the subject’s treatment and baseline covariate values. Each subject contributes one joint probability across their observed post-baseline visits, with missing visits marginalized. The resulting predictive mass functions are compared with respect to counting measure on integer score vectors. The comparison therefore uses the logarithmic scoring rule for the predictive distribution of the recorded score categories (Gneiting and Raftery,, 2007).

For the Gaussian model, the joint interval probability is a normal rectangle probability on the original scale. The intervals for scores 00 and 6363 are [−0.5,0.5)\left[-0.5,0.5\right) and [62.5,63.5)\left[62.5,63.5\right), respectively. Gaussian probability outside the valid score categories is retained in the predictive distribution: predictions are neither clipped nor renormalized to the range 00 to 6363.

In this application, the common latent thresholds are a=Φ−1​(0.5/64)a=\Phi^{-1}\left(0.5/64\right) and b=Φ−1​(63.5/64)b=\Phi^{-1}\left(63.5/64\right). The continuous bounded comparator uses

h⁡(y)=Φ−1​(y+0.564),Yi​trep=64​Φ​(Hi​trep)−0.5.h\left(y\right)=\Phi^{-1}\left(\frac{y+0.5}{64}\right),\qquad Y_{it}^{\mathrm{rep}}=64\Phi\left(H_{it}^{\mathrm{rep}}\right)-0.5. (62)

Its continuous support is (−0.5,63.5)\left(-0.5,63.5\right), and it has no atoms at 00 or 6363. In its fitting likelihood, both endpoints are evaluated as finite transformed values, h⁡(0)=ah\left(0\right)=a and h⁡(63)=bh\left(63\right)=b, with the corresponding Jacobian. The Gaussian fitting likelihood also evaluates densities at these endpoints. The mixed-boundary model instead maps latent values at or below aa to 00, values at or above bb to 6363, and interior values through the same inverse transformation. Its fitting likelihood integrates the latent tail regions for exact boundary observations; see Web Appendix C.

Under either bounded model, the latent interval for the predictive score at an observed integer yy is

[Φ−1​(y64),Φ−1​(y+164)),\left[\Phi^{-1}\left(\frac{y}{64}\right),\Phi^{-1}\left(\frac{y+1}{64}\right)\right), (63)

with infinite endpoints interpreted in the usual way. For the mixed-boundary model, the endpoint intervals include the corresponding atoms. The two bounded models thus use identical rectangle limits, but their posterior distributions differ because their fitting likelihoods treat exact bounds differently. This comparison evaluates prediction at the recorded score resolution; it does not distinguish an atom from continuous probability within the same endpoint interval.

C.2 Prediction with a subject left out

Let 𝒟−i\mathcal{D}_{-i} denote the observed outcomes of the other n−1n-1 subjects. Conditional on treatment and baseline covariates, the contribution for subject ii is

ℓi​m=log⁡{∫qi​m​(θm)​pm​(θm|𝒟−i)​d​θm},ELPD^m=∑i=1nℓ^i​m.\ell_{im}=\log\left\{\int q_{im}\left(\theta_{m}\right)p_{m}\left(\theta_{m}\middle|\mathcal{D}_{-i}\right)\,d\theta_{m}\right\},\qquad\widehat{\mathrm{ELPD}}_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{\ell}_{im}. (64)

All observed outcomes for the held-out subject are excluded from fitting. Baseline centering is held fixed across folds. Higher ELPD indicates better prediction of the observed score intervals.

Let SS denote the number of retained posterior draws used for the predictive comparison. Write Li​m​(θm)L_{im}\left(\theta_{m}\right) for the subject’s original observed likelihood contribution, including integration over latent variables associated with observed boundaries. With draws θm(s)\theta_{m}^{\left(s\right)} from the posterior fitted to all subjects, the importance ratios are proportional to 1/Li​m​(θm(s))1/L_{im}\left(\theta_{m}^{\left(s\right)}\right). After PSIS smoothing and normalization, the weights w~i​m(s)\widetilde{w}_{im}^{\left(s\right)} give

ℓ^i​m=log⁡{∑s=1Sw~i​m(s)​qi​m​(θm(s))},∑s=1Sw~i​m(s)=1.\widehat{\ell}_{im}=\log\left\{\sum_{s=1}^{S}\widetilde{w}_{im}^{\left(s\right)}q_{im}\left(\theta_{m}^{\left(s\right)}\right)\right\},\qquad\sum_{s=1}^{S}\widetilde{w}_{im}^{\left(s\right)}=1. (65)

The fitting likelihood determines the weights, whereas the common interval probability determines the predictive score. Substituting interval probabilities for the likelihood in the importance ratios would not recover the leave-one-subject-out posterior of the fitted model. When the PSIS diagnostics were inadequate, we refitted the model without subject ii and averaged interval probabilities using equal weights over all draws from that refit (Vehtari et al.,, 2017; Vehtari et al.,, 2025).

C.3 Uncertainty in model differences

For models mm and m′m^{\prime}, define di=ℓ^i​m−ℓ^i​m′d_{i}=\widehat{\ell}_{im}-\widehat{\ell}_{im^{\prime}} and d¯=n−1​∑i=1ndi\bar{d}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i}. We report the ELPD difference and its approximate SE as

Δ^m,m′=∑i=1ndi,SE^​(Δ^m,m′)={nn−1​∑i=1n(di−d¯)2}1/2.\widehat{\Delta}_{m,m^{\prime}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i},\qquad\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}\left(\widehat{\Delta}_{m,m^{\prime}}\right)=\left\{\frac{n}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(d_{i}-\bar{d}\right)^{2}\right\}^{1/2}. (66)

The SE of an individual model’s ELPD is obtained by replacing did_{i} with ℓ^i​m\widehat{\ell}_{im} in the same expression. Pairwise SEs use the differences within subjects and cannot be obtained by treating the model estimates as independent (Vehtari et al.,, 2017; Vehtari et al.,, 2025). These SEs describe variation across subjects, rather than Monte Carlo or numerical integration error. The comparison concerns observed outcome prediction under the fitted working models and does not test the reference-based assumptions about missing outcomes.
