Web Appendix B Simulation study design and supplementary results

This appendix gives the simulation inputs and supplementary numerical results for Studies 1 to 3.

B.1 Setup for Simulation Studies 1 and 2

Studies 1 and 2 used the common bounded scale

Yi​t∈[0,63],Y_{it}\in\left[0,63\right], (67)

with lower bound L=0L=0, upper bound U=63U=63, unit score step s=1s=1, and T=5T=5 post-baseline visits. The unit step size was used only to define the threshold probabilities through the implied half-step boundaries of the underlying score grid.

The half-step construction of Section 4.1 gave pL=0.5/64p_{L}=0.5/64 and pU=63.5/64p_{U}=63.5/64, with latent thresholds a=Φ−1​(pL)a=\Phi^{-1}\left(p_{L}\right) and b=Φ−1​(pU)b=\Phi^{-1}\left(p_{U}\right). Accordingly, the thresholded latent Gaussian generator produced a continuous interior on (0,63)\left(0,63\right) together with positive mass at the bounds, rather than outcomes restricted to the full integer lattice.

In Studies 1 and 2, each fitted model used two Markov chains with 1,000 warmup iterations and 1,000 retained post-warmup iterations per chain. All post-warmup draws were retained for inference. Posterior computation was carried out in Stan using dynamic Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with a target acceptance probability of 0.950.95 and a maximum tree depth of 1010.

B.2 Simulation Study 1: construction of the primary model scenarios

Let s∈{1,…,4}s\in\left\{1,\dots,4\right\} index the Study 1 scenario and let t∈{1,…,T}t\in\left\{1,\dots,T\right\} index visit. Scenario ss was defined through probabilities of the lower and upper bounds in the control arm on the observed scale, together with a vector of standardized treatment shifts across visits, 𝜿(s)\bm{\kappa}^{\left(s\right)}, and an AR(1) correlation parameter ρ(s)\rho^{\left(s\right)}. Equivalently, each scenario was determined by the vectors

𝝅0L,(s)=(π01L,(s),…,π0​TL,(s))⊤,𝝅0U,(s)=(π01U,(s),…,π0​TU,(s))⊤,𝜿(s)=(κ1(s),…,κT(s))⊤,\bm{\pi}_{0}^{L,\left(s\right)}=\left(\pi_{01}^{L,\left(s\right)},\dots,\pi_{0T}^{L,\left(s\right)}\right)^{\top},\qquad\bm{\pi}_{0}^{U,\left(s\right)}=\left(\pi_{01}^{U,\left(s\right)},\dots,\pi_{0T}^{U,\left(s\right)}\right)^{\top},\qquad\bm{\kappa}^{\left(s\right)}=\left(\kappa_{1}^{\left(s\right)},\dots,\kappa_{T}^{\left(s\right)}\right)^{\top}, (68)

together with ρ(s)\rho^{\left(s\right)}. Here, π0​tL,(s)\pi_{0t}^{L,\left(s\right)} and π0​tU,(s)\pi_{0t}^{U,\left(s\right)} denote the probabilities that the outcome equals the lower and upper bounds, respectively, in the control arm at visit tt under scenario ss.

For scenario ss, let

ztL,(s)=Φ−1​(π0​tL,(s))andztU,(s)=Φ−1​(1−π0​tU,(s)).z_{t}^{L,\left(s\right)}=\Phi^{-1}\left(\pi_{0t}^{L,\left(s\right)}\right)\qquad\text{and}\qquad z_{t}^{U,\left(s\right)}=\Phi^{-1}\left(1-\pi_{0t}^{U,\left(s\right)}\right). (69)

Solving the normal quantile equations a=αt(s)+σt(s)​ztL,(s)a=\alpha_{t}^{\left(s\right)}+\sigma_{t}^{\left(s\right)}z_{t}^{L,\left(s\right)} and b=αt(s)+σt(s)​ztU,(s)b=\alpha_{t}^{\left(s\right)}+\sigma_{t}^{\left(s\right)}z_{t}^{U,\left(s\right)} gave the marginal latent SDs and control arm latent intercepts:

σt(s)=b−aztU,(s)−ztL,(s),αt(s)=a−σt(s)​ztL,(s).\sigma_{t}^{\left(s\right)}=\frac{b-a}{z_{t}^{U,\left(s\right)}-z_{t}^{L,\left(s\right)}},\qquad\alpha_{t}^{\left(s\right)}=a-\sigma_{t}^{\left(s\right)}z_{t}^{L,\left(s\right)}. (70)

By construction, this gives the desired control-arm boundary probabilities under the thresholded latent Gaussian model.

Treatment separation was introduced through

δt(s)=κt(s)​σt(s),\delta_{t}^{\left(s\right)}=\kappa_{t}^{\left(s\right)}\sigma_{t}^{\left(s\right)}, (71)

so that the visit-specific latent means were

μ0​t(s)=αt(s)andμ1​t(s)=αt(s)+δt(s).\mu_{0t}^{\left(s\right)}=\alpha_{t}^{\left(s\right)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mu_{1t}^{\left(s\right)}=\alpha_{t}^{\left(s\right)}+\delta_{t}^{\left(s\right)}. (72)

Hence, the active arm boundary probabilities were implied quantities rather than primary design inputs.

The within-subject covariance matrix for scenario ss was

Σ(s)=D(s)​R​(ρ(s))​D(s),\Sigma^{\left(s\right)}=D^{\left(s\right)}R\left(\rho^{\left(s\right)}\right)D^{\left(s\right)}, (73)

where

D(s)=diag⁡(σ1(s),…,σT(s)),D^{\left(s\right)}=\operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_{1}^{\left(s\right)},\dots,\sigma_{T}^{\left(s\right)}\right), (74)

and

Rt​u​(ρ(s))=(ρ(s))|t−u|,t,u=1,…,T.R_{tu}\left(\rho^{\left(s\right)}\right)=\left(\rho^{\left(s\right)}\right)^{\left|t-u\right|},\qquad t,u=1,\dots,T. (75)

The four Study 1 scenarios were chosen for distinct purposes. SparseBoundary provides a benchmark with outcomes concentrated in the interior and only mild boundary accumulation. ModerateFloor was chosen to mimic progressive accumulation near the lower bound. AggressiveCeiling stresses the methods under increasing accumulation at the upper bound. AggressiveBothBounds is a deliberately difficult two-sided setting with appreciable mass at both bounds.

After generating complete data, we imposed monotone dropout with a vector of hazards for each scenario,

𝒉(s)=(h1(s),…,hT(s))⊤.\bm{h}^{\left(s\right)}=\left(h_{1}^{\left(s\right)},\dots,h_{T}^{\left(s\right)}\right)^{\top}. (76)

Specifically,

𝒉(SparseBoundary)=(0.00,0.03,0.05,0.07,0.09)⊤,\bm{h}^{\left(\mathrm{SparseBoundary}\right)}=\left(0.00,0.03,0.05,0.07,0.09\right)^{\top}, (77)

whereas

𝒉(s)=(0.00,0.04,0.06,0.08,0.10)⊤,\displaystyle\bm{h}^{\left(s\right)}=\left(0.00,0.04,0.06,0.08,0.10\right)^{\top}, (78)
s∈{ModerateFloor,AggressiveCeiling,AggressiveBothBounds}.\displaystyle s\in\left\{\mathrm{ModerateFloor},\mathrm{AggressiveCeiling},\mathrm{AggressiveBothBounds}\right\}.

Because dropout depended only on visit and not on latent outcomes, treatment arm, or latent random effects, it was a simple special case of the MAR assumption used in the primary model. The first visit was fully observed. At each subsequent visit tt, subjects who had not previously dropped out were independently assigned dropout with probability ht(s)h_{t}^{\left(s\right)}. When dropout occurred at visit tt, the outcome at that visit and all subsequent outcomes were set to missing. Thus, ht(s)h_{t}^{\left(s\right)} is a conditional dropout probability among subjects still in follow-up, rather than the marginal probability of a missing outcome at visit tt.

For the continuous bounded comparator in Study 1, exact scores of 00 and 6363 were replaced by 0.50.5 and 62.562.5, respectively, while interior scores were unchanged. Denoting these adjusted scores by Y†Y^{\dagger}, we fitted a Gaussian model to H=Φ−1​(Y†/63)H=\Phi^{-1}\left(Y^{\dagger}/63\right) and calculated model-implied means on the observed scale using the inverse map Y=63​Φ​(H)Y=63\Phi\left(H\right). This comparator differs from the continuous bounded comparator used in the application, whose transformation is defined in Appendix C.

Although the latent parameter and boundary probability tables focus on calibration of the proposed mixed-boundary model, the retained Study 1 tables also include recovery of arm means on the observed scale across all three working models, since this comparison more directly shows how modeling that respects the support affects fit on the observed scale. The exact Study 1 inputs are reported in Web Table 1, the resulting mean missingness proportions in Web Table 2, the retained latent and boundary recovery summaries in Web Table 3, Web Table 4, Web Table 5, and Web Table 6, and the comparison of arm means on the observed scale across working models in Web Table 7.

B.3 Simulation Study 2: support templates, truth rules, and reported summaries

Let s∈{MF,ABB}s\in\left\{\mathrm{MF},\mathrm{ABB}\right\} index the support template, where MF\mathrm{MF} denotes ModerateFloor and ABB\mathrm{ABB} denotes AggressiveBothBounds. Let r∈{MAR,WJ2R0.50,J2R,CR}r\in\left\{\mathrm{MAR},\mathrm{WJ2R}_{0.50},\mathrm{J2R},\mathrm{CR}\right\} index the truth rule for the active arm after the trigger. Each Study 2 scenario was therefore the pair (s,r)\left(s,r\right).

Support template ss was defined by the six inputs

𝝅0L,(s),𝝅0U,(s),𝜿(s),ρ(s),𝜼(s),𝝀(s),\bm{\pi}_{0}^{L,\left(s\right)},\qquad\bm{\pi}_{0}^{U,\left(s\right)},\qquad\bm{\kappa}^{\left(s\right)},\qquad\rho^{\left(s\right)},\qquad\bm{\eta}^{\left(s\right)},\qquad\bm{\lambda}^{\left(s\right)}, (79)

where 𝝅0L,(s)=(π01L,(s),…,π0​TL,(s))⊤\bm{\pi}_{0}^{L,\left(s\right)}=\left(\pi_{01}^{L,\left(s\right)},\dots,\pi_{0T}^{L,\left(s\right)}\right)^{\top} and 𝝅0U,(s)=(π01U,(s),…,π0​TU,(s))⊤\bm{\pi}_{0}^{U,\left(s\right)}=\left(\pi_{01}^{U,\left(s\right)},\dots,\pi_{0T}^{U,\left(s\right)}\right)^{\top} are the vectors of probabilities of the lower and upper bounds in the control arm, 𝜿(s)=(κ1(s),…,κT(s))⊤\bm{\kappa}^{\left(s\right)}=\left(\kappa_{1}^{\left(s\right)},\dots,\kappa_{T}^{\left(s\right)}\right)^{\top} is the vector of standardized treatment shifts, ρ(s)\rho^{\left(s\right)} is the AR(1) correlation parameter, 𝜼(s)=(η1(s),…,ηT(s))⊤\bm{\eta}^{\left(s\right)}=\left(\eta_{1}^{\left(s\right)},\dots,\eta_{T}^{\left(s\right)}\right)^{\top} gives the probabilities of intermittent missingness before the final tail, and 𝝀(s)=(λ1(s),…,λT(s))⊤\bm{\lambda}^{\left(s\right)}=\left(\lambda_{1}^{\left(s\right)},\dots,\lambda_{T}^{\left(s\right)}\right)^{\top} gives the dropout hazards for the final missing tail.

The latent mean vectors and covariance matrix under template ss were obtained from the same construction as in Study 1, namely through δt(s)=κt(s)​σt(s)\delta_{t}^{\left(s\right)}=\kappa_{t}^{\left(s\right)}\sigma_{t}^{\left(s\right)} and Σ(s)=D(s)​R​(ρ(s))​D(s)\Sigma^{\left(s\right)}=D^{\left(s\right)}R\left(\rho^{\left(s\right)}\right)D^{\left(s\right)}. The support template, therefore, determined the boundary pattern, structure of treatment shifts, covariance structure, and missingness design, whereas the truth rule rr determined only the distribution of missing outcomes in the active arm after the trigger.

The ModerateFloor template was intended to represent increasing floor accumulation with limited mass at the upper bound. The AggressiveBothBounds template was intended to represent a more difficult two-sided boundary setting and therefore used higher dropout hazards for the final missing tail to increase the influence of the sensitivity rules. The exact template inputs, combinations of truth rules, and scenario labels are listed in Web Table 8.

The missingness pattern was generated separately for each subject before generating the latent outcomes. We first selected an initial dropout visit sequentially, with λt(s)\lambda_{t}^{\left(s\right)} giving the probability of dropout at visit tt conditional on no earlier dropout. The initial dropout visit was set to T+1T+1 if no dropout occurred. All outcomes from the initial dropout visit onward were designated missing. Conditional on that visit, each earlier outcome was independently designated missing with probability ηt(s)\eta_{t}^{\left(s\right)}. The same probabilities were used in both treatment arms. After combining these two components, the sensitivity trigger was determined from the last observed visit. Consequently, additional missing values immediately preceding the initially generated dropout tail were included in the final missing tail and could move the trigger earlier. Additional missing values at the end of follow-up could also create a final missing tail when no initial dropout had occurred.

For subject ii, let

𝒪iobs={t∈{1,…,T}:Ri​t=1}\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\left\{t\in\left\{1,\dots,T\right\}:R_{it}=1\right\} (80)

denote the observed post-baseline visit set after imposing missingness. If 𝒪iobs=∅\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\varnothing, we set τi=1\tau_{i}=1. Otherwise, let

tilast=max⁡𝒪iobs,t_{i}^{\mathrm{last}}=\max\mathcal{O}_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}, (81)

and define

τi={tilast+1,if ​tilast<T,T+1,if ​tilast=T.\tau_{i}=\begin{cases}t_{i}^{\mathrm{last}}+1,&\text{if }t_{i}^{\mathrm{last}}<T,\\ T+1,&\text{if }t_{i}^{\mathrm{last}}=T.\end{cases} (82)

Thus, missing values at visits t<τit<\tau_{i}, before the trigger, were generated under MAR within each arm, whereas missing values at visits t≥τit\geq\tau_{i} in the final monotone tail of the active arm followed the truth rule for that scenario. The resulting mean missingness proportions are reported in Web Table 9.

Each dataset in Study 2 was analyzed only with the proposed mixed-boundary model. The fitted model was therefore held fixed across sensitivity analyses, and only the posterior predictive completion rule was varied. The analysis rules were MAR, weighted J2R with ω=0.50\omega=0.50, J2R, and CR. The retained Study 2 summary reports the difference between the complete-data arm means on the observed scale at the final scheduled visit; see Web Table 10.

B.4 Simulation Study 3: design and computational details

Each replicate contained 100 subjects randomized equally between arms, four post-baseline visits, and an independent baseline covariate Bi∼𝒩⁡(0,1)B_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,1\right). This covariate was fully observed and was not itself a bounded outcome. The MAR latent outcomes were generated as

Hi​tMAR=αt+βt​Bi+Ai​δt+εi​t,H_{it}^{\mathrm{MAR}}=\alpha_{t}+\beta_{t}B_{i}+A_{i}\delta_{t}+\varepsilon_{it}, (83)

with

𝜶\displaystyle\bm{\alpha} =(−0.8,−1.1,−1.3,−1.5)⊤,\displaystyle=\left(-0.8,-1.1,-1.3,-1.5\right)^{\top}, (84)
𝜷\displaystyle\bm{\beta} =(0.35,0.35,0.30,0.30)⊤,\displaystyle=\left(0.35,0.35,0.30,0.30\right)^{\top},
𝜹\displaystyle\bm{\delta} =(−0.15,−0.30,−0.45,−0.55)⊤.\displaystyle=\left(-0.15,-0.30,-0.45,-0.55\right)^{\top}.

The residual covariance had marginal SDs (0.9,0.95,1,1)\left(0.9,0.95,1,1\right) and AR(1) correlation parameter 0.60.6. Gaussian errors followed 𝒩4​(𝟎,Σ)\mathcal{N}_{4}\left(\mathbf{0},\Sigma\right). Heavy-tailed errors were generated as εi=3/Vi​Zi\varepsilon_{i}=\sqrt{3/V_{i}}\,Z_{i}, where Zi∼𝒩4​(𝟎,Σ)Z_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}_{4}\left(\mathbf{0},\Sigma\right) and Vi∼χ52V_{i}\sim\chi^{2}_{5} were independent. A single scale factor was shared across visits within each subject, giving multivariate t5t_{5} errors with covariance Σ\Sigma. Outcomes were obtained using the threshold map of Section 4.1, with L=0L=0, U=63U=63, pL=0.5/64p_{L}=0.5/64, and pU=63.5/64p_{U}=63.5/64, without rounding interior values.

Missingness patterns were generated independently of baseline and latent errors. The visit-specific hazards for starting a monotone missing tail were (0,0.12,0.14,0.20)\left(0,0.12,0.14,0.20\right); before that tail, intermittent missingness probabilities were (0,0.05,0.05,0)\left(0,0.05,0.05,0\right). For each subject, the missingness pattern was sampled from the exact pattern probabilities implied by the sequential dropout and independent gap construction described for Study 2. The sensitivity trigger was the visit after the last observed outcome. J2R truth was obtained by subtracting Ai​δtA_{i}\delta_{t} from the MAR latent outcome at each missing visit from the trigger onward. Paired MAR and J2R truths therefore shared the same observed data, allowing posterior fits to be reused. Population targets were calculated by numerical integration over the outcome and baseline distributions and exact averaging over the probabilities of the missingness patterns.

Both imputation models retained Gaussian working distributions, so the t5t_{5} scenarios assessed distributional misspecification. Missing values in the reference arm and gaps before the trigger in the active arm were imputed under MAR; the sensitivity rules applied to the final missing tail in the active arm. Each fit used four chains, 500 warmup iterations, and 1,000 post-warmup iterations per chain, with adaptation target 0.950.95 and maximum tree depth 1212. All 4,000 post-warmup draws were used. The final 1,200 fits passed the diagnostic checks, with no divergences or hits at the maximum tree depth.

To reduce computation, MMRM estimates and restricted maximum likelihood covariance estimates for complete datasets were calculated using the equivalent multivariate regression formulas, checked against nlme::gls. The regression design matrix had one row per subject and three columns representing the intercept, baseline covariate, and treatment indicator, with separate regression coefficients for each visit. Thus, the complete-data analysis had 100−3=97100-3=97 residual degrees of freedom. Its confidence interval for the treatment contrast at visit 4 used the corresponding estimate and SE with a Student tt critical value based on these degrees of freedom. For the imputation analyses, estimates and variance estimates were combined across completed datasets separately at each visit using Rubin’s rules, with the conventional degrees of freedom for multiple imputation. At nominal 95%95\% coverage, 300 replicates give a Monte Carlo SE of approximately 1.26 percentage points.

Each scenario uses 300 replicates with 100 subjects (50 per arm). Δ\Delta is the fixed population mean difference, active minus reference, on the bounded outcome scale at visit 4. Emp. SD is the empirical standard deviation of the estimates; Mean SE is the average estimated standard error; Cov. is empirical coverage of nominal 95%95\% intervals. Both imputation methods use an MMRM on the observed scale and Rubin’s rules with 4,000 imputations per replicate. Complete data denotes the same MMRM fitted before masking outcomes. The interval for the treatment contrast at visit 4 uses the corresponding MMRM estimate and SE with a Student tt critical value based on 97 residual degrees of freedom. The Monte Carlo SE of coverage at 95%95\% is 1.26 percentage points. Coverage under rules that differ from the truth is descriptive and is not expected to equal 95%95\%. WJ2R(0.50) uses weight ω=0.50\omega=0.50.

Web Appendix C Predictive comparison: likelihood and computation

Appendix Cdefines the common interval score. This appendix describes the original observed likelihood used to obtain the importance weights and the numerical evaluation of both quantities.

C.1 Observed likelihood for the mixed-boundary model

For subject ii, let ℐi\mathcal{I}_{i}, ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i}, and 𝒰i\mathcal{U}_{i} denote observed visits in the interior, at the lower bound, and at the upper bound. Write ℬi=ℒi∪𝒰i\mathcal{B}_{i}=\mathcal{L}_{i}\cup\mathcal{U}_{i} and let hi,ℐi=gi​(Yi,ℐi)h_{i,\mathcal{I}_{i}}=g_{i}\left(Y_{i,\mathcal{I}_{i}}\right). Define ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} as the rectangle requiring Hi​t≤aiH_{it}\leq a_{i} for t∈ℒit\in\mathcal{L}_{i} and Hi​t≥biH_{it}\geq b_{i} for t∈𝒰it\in\mathcal{U}_{i}. Write μi=μi​Ai\mu_{i}=\mu_{iA_{i}} for the mean vector corresponding to subject ii’s assigned arm. Suppressing the model subscript, the observed likelihood contribution is

Li​(θ)=\displaystyle L_{i}\left(\theta\right)={} ϕ|ℐi|​(hi,ℐi,μi,ℐi,Σℐi​ℐi)​|Ji​(hi,ℐi)|\displaystyle\phi_{\left|\mathcal{I}_{i}\right|}\left(h_{i,\mathcal{I}_{i}};\mu_{i,\mathcal{I}_{i}},\Sigma_{\mathcal{I}_{i}\mathcal{I}_{i}}\right)\left|J_{i}\left(h_{i,\mathcal{I}_{i}}\right)\right| (85)
×Pr(Hi,ℬi∈ℛi|Hi,ℐi=hi,ℐi,Ai,Xi,θ),\displaystyle\times\Pr\left(H_{i,\mathcal{B}_{i}}\in\mathcal{R}_{i}\middle|H_{i,\mathcal{I}_{i}}=h_{i,\mathcal{I}_{i}},A_{i},X_{i},\theta\right),

where ϕd\phi_{d} denotes a dd-dimensional normal density and

|Ji​(hi,ℐi)|=∏t∈ℐipUi−pLiUi−Li​1ϕ⁡(hi​t).\left|J_{i}\left(h_{i,\mathcal{I}_{i}}\right)\right|=\prod_{t\in\mathcal{I}_{i}}\frac{p_{U_{i}}-p_{L_{i}}}{U_{i}-L_{i}}\frac{1}{\phi\left(h_{it}\right)}. (86)

The final factor is a conditional normal rectangle probability. If there are no observed boundaries, it equals 11. If there are no observed interior values, the density and Jacobian factors are omitted and the likelihood is the marginal rectangle probability for the observed boundary events. Missing visits are marginalized in each case. The boundary latent values sampled during fitting are therefore integrated out when computing the importance weights.

For the Gaussian comparator, the observed likelihood is the joint normal density of the observed scores. For the continuous bounded comparator, it is the joint normal density of the transformed observed scores multiplied by the Jacobian, including at scores 00 and 6363. In the application, the Jacobian contribution per visit is 1/{64​ϕ​(hi​t)}1/\left\{64\phi\left(h_{it}\right)\right\}. The same observed visit set is used for the fitting likelihood and the common interval score.

C.2 Numerical evaluation and diagnostics

Normal rectangle probabilities were evaluated in R using randomized integration through mvtnorm, targeting relative error 10−510^{-5}. When the initial integrations did not meet this criterion, conditional Gaussian quadrature was used, with agreement checked at three successive resolutions and a bound on omitted tail probability. An unresolved integration stopped the calculation. The application requires rectangles of at most four dimensions. Integration was parallelized across posterior draws, and completed calculations were saved for reuse. These integrations are required for the predictive comparison, not for fitting the augmented primary model or generating reference-based imputations.

PSIS weights were obtained with loo::psis from the negative observed log-likelihood contributions, with relative effective sample sizes accounting for MCMC dependence (Vehtari et al.,, 2025). A model was refitted after removing subject ii when the Pareto diagnostic was at least min⁡{0.7,1−1/log10⁡(S)}\min\left\{0.7,1-1/\log_{10}\left(S\right)\right\}, the PSIS effective sample size was below 100100, or either diagnostic was nonfinite. Each application model and explicit leave-one-subject-out refit used four chains, with 1,000 warmup iterations and 1,000 post-warmup iterations per chain, a target acceptance probability of 0.990.99, and a maximum tree depth of 1212. The predictive comparison used all 4,000 post-warmup draws from each fit. The number of explicit refits was 33 for the continuous bounded model, 44 for the mixed-boundary model, and 11 for the Gaussian model. These refits replace the importance approximation for the affected subjects; they are separate from the 5050 completed datasets used for the downstream MMRM analysis.

We assessed agreement between MCMC chains using the rank-normalized split R^\widehat{R} diagnostic, a refinement of the potential scale reduction factor (Vehtari et al.,, 2021). The reported MCMC checks required R^≤1.01\widehat{R}\leq 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes of at least 100100 for the monitored nonconstant structural parameters, no divergent transitions or maximum tree depth hits, and an energy Bayesian fraction of missing information of at least 0.30.3 in each chain. All reported checks passed. Subject contributions were also accompanied by Monte Carlo SE estimates accounting for MCMC dependence; these estimates do not include numerical integration error and are distinct from the SEs of ELPD differences across subjects. Approximate Monte Carlo SEs of the overall ELPD differences, accounting for dependence among subject contributions sharing a posterior fit, ranged from 0.310.31 to 0.340.34. These estimates condition on the estimated PSIS weights and refit decisions and exclude numerical integration error.

Web Appendix D Model comparisons and sensitivity analyses

Under MAR, we compared the mixed-boundary and continuous bounded models for the same subjects with missing BDI-II at month 8: 20 in TAU and 25 in BtheB. For each of all 4,000 retained posterior draws, we calculated each subject’s conditional probability of an outcome equal to zero and of an outcome in [−0.5,0.5)\left[-0.5,0.5\right) using normal CDFs, conditional on baseline BDI-II and the observed history. The mixed-boundary calculation included the corresponding posterior draws of latent values for observed boundary scores. Probabilities were averaged across the subjects with missing scores within each arm. We report posterior means and 95% credible intervals for these average conditional probabilities, rather than intervals for proportions in completed datasets.

The mixed-boundary model assigned positive probability to outcomes equal to zero, whereas the continuous bounded model has no probability mass at zero. Both models assigned positive probability to the common interval representing a rounded zero (Web Table 12). The continuous bounded predictions were not clipped before calculating these probabilities.

We additionally examined sensitivity to the threshold specification using extensions of c=0.25c=0.25 and c=1.00c=1.00 points, compared with the original c=0.50c=0.50. The lower and upper threshold probabilities were pL=c/(63+2​c)p_{L}=c/\left(63+2c\right) and pU=1−pLp_{U}=1-p_{L}, with latent thresholds obtained by applying Φ−1\Phi^{-1}. The observed bounds remained 0 and 63, and the recorded score resolution was unchanged. We refitted the mixed-boundary model under each alternative, updating the interior transformation and Jacobian while retaining the same priors and MCMC settings.

For each threshold specification, we used all 4,000 posterior draws after warmup to generate completed datasets under MAR, WJ2R(0.50), J2R, and CR for BtheB, with TAU under MAR. All 97 retained subjects were included, with observed outcomes held fixed. The completed arm means and proportions of zeros at month 8 were summarized as in Figure 5 and showed little change across the specifications examined (Web Table 13). All reported fit and profile diagnostic checks passed.
